01.1 — Line 1▶

01.1 — Line 1

001爻 Case ID: XCASE-H01-L1 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-01-02 | Event ID: E56 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 潛龍勿用，陽在下也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「潛藏的龍，時機未到，不宜施展。」《象傳》解釋：陽爻還在最下方，時機尚未成熟。

Historical event | Short narrative

In the state of Jin, disputes over succession forced Chong'er, a member of the ruling house, to leave his homeland. Departure did not give him another court, an established army, or a secure place in which to exercise political authority. He travelled with followers through a succession of states, and every new arrival placed practical questions before the group. They needed permission to remain, food and other support, and a host prepared to receive a person whose political future remained uncertain. The welcome was not uniform. Some rulers provided assistance, while elsewhere Chong'er and his companions received less favourable treatment. The difference mattered because the travelling group could not simply command another state to supply it. Decisions made by each host affected where the exiles could stay and what help they could seek next. The followers who continued with Chong'er also had to endure a journey whose outcome could not be settled in advance. Over time, the political circumstances in Jin changed. Support from Qin eventually became decisive in enabling Chong'er to return. With that outside assistance and a changed situation at home, he re-entered Jin and took the throne, becoming Duke Wen of Jin. His accession was therefore the outcome of a prolonged sequence: an initial succession struggle, years away from Jin, relationships with several host states, and the opportunity created by Qin's intervention. The historical account records that progression, but it does not supply a complete itinerary of each day's travel or every private exchange among the exiles. Nor does a successful return mean that the exiled prince had known at departure that he would rule. What can be followed is the changing relationship between his immediate circumstances and the assistance available to him. His position altered only after those circumstances, and the actions of other participants, allowed a return to Jin.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The first line of Qian describes a dragon still below the surface. Its Small Image commentary says that the active force remains in a lower position. Chong'er's exile offers a historical comparison, not proof that he consulted this passage. He left Jin during a succession dispute, moved among other states and depended upon the treatment of hosts and the continued support of followers. Only after years abroad, with assistance from Qin and altered conditions within Jin, did he return to become Duke Wen. For a modern reader, the central distinction is between a future possibility and the authority available today. A title, claim or long-term objective cannot replace food, shelter, reliable partners and an opening through which a decision can actually be carried out. In the historical account, those conditions did not arrive together or on a predetermined schedule. The lesson is not to predict a favourable ending from a hexagram. It is to distinguish what the sources record, what circumstances presently permit, and what remains outside one's control.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

01.2 — Line 2▶

01.2 — Line 2

002爻 Case ID: XCASE-H01-L2 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-01-03 | Event ID: E01 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 見龍在田，德施普也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「龍出現在田野，適宜拜見有德位的大人。」《象傳》解釋：德行已能廣泛影響眾人。

Historical event | Short narrative

As the Qin dynasty collapsed, competing armies advanced toward the former imperial heartland of Guanzhong. Liu Bang entered a region where people had experienced Qin administration and now faced a different armed force. For the residents, the change of control raised immediate questions. Which laws would remain? How would the soldiers behave? What would happen to families and local communities under a new military presence? After entering Guanzhong, Liu Bang announced a simplified set of rules known as the Three Articles of Agreement. He communicated the arrangement to local elders, replacing the expectation of numerous harsh provisions with a small number of clearly stated prohibitions. The announcement was a political act as well as a statement of law: inhabitants could hear what the new authorities claimed they would require, while Liu Bang's troops still had to conduct themselves in accordance with that claim. Establishing rules did not establish a settled dynasty. Xiang Yu and other commanders continued to exercise considerable military power, and control of territory beyond Guanzhong remained contested. Liu Bang's position therefore depended both on relations with the population already under his control and on the conflicts that continued elsewhere. The public promise could be judged through subsequent encounters between civilians and soldiers; its delivery was not completed by the announcement alone. The sequence is clear without imagining individual conversations. Qin authority disintegrated, Liu Bang's forces entered the region, an abbreviated legal arrangement was announced, and the wider struggle for power continued. The account provides an example of how a new commander introduced administrative expectations while the military outcome remained unresolved. It does not show that every resident welcomed the change or that the three rules, by themselves, determined who would eventually rule China. Those questions extend beyond this single episode and belong to the subsequent political and military history of the period.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The second line of Qian turns to a dragon visible in the field; the Small Image says that virtue can now extend outward. Liu Bang's entry into Guanzhong can be read beside this idea. After Qin authority broke down, his army entered a populated region and announced the Three Articles of Agreement. Residents received a simpler statement of the conduct and offences the new authorities intended to regulate. The announcement mattered because people needed to know how the arriving armed force would govern. But this is a retrospective analogy. There is no claim that Liu Bang used the Small Image to design his rules. The announcement did not conclude the struggle for political control, and later conduct still had to match the public promise. In a present-day organisation, a statement of values becomes meaningful only when those affected can observe the rules in action. Ask who hears the announcement, who applies it, and how inconsistencies can be challenged. A visible beginning does not equal a finished system.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

01.3 — Line 3▶

01.3 — Line 3

003爻 Case ID: XCASE-H01-L3 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-01-04 | Event ID: E32 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 終日乾乾，反復道也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「君子整天勤奮不懈，夜晚仍警惕；雖有危險，沒有災咎。」《象傳》解釋：走的是回復正道的路。

Historical event | Short narrative

By 1938, the war between China and Japan had already brought major changes to the military situation. Different fronts had experienced different results, and the mobilisation of soldiers and civilians had become a central issue. Judgements about the likely course of the war varied. Some observers focused on immediate battlefield outcomes, while the conflict itself continued across a much longer period than any single engagement. In this setting, Mao Zedong wrote On Protracted War. The text examined the conditions of the two sides and argued that the conflict should be understood over time. Instead of treating the outcome of a particular battle as the final measure of the war, the argument described successive stages and the changing relationship between military strength, organisation and sustained resistance. It was a contemporary strategic analysis directed at a war that was still under way. The publication did not cause the fighting to stop or settle the problems faced by individual units. Military organisations still had to provide food and equipment, maintain command arrangements, and respond to changing circumstances on their fronts. Political decisions and international developments would also affect the course of the conflict. The staged argument gave readers a way to organise questions about duration and changing capabilities, but the later history cannot be treated as if it were already known when the text appeared. The story begins with an ongoing war and disputed assessments of its future. It continues with the drafting and circulation of a proposal for understanding a prolonged conflict. Its aftermath lies in the continued military and political activity that the publication did not replace. The surviving work allows the author's public reasoning to be studied directly. It does not provide a day-by-day record of all subsequent operations, and later victory cannot retrospectively turn every statement in the 1938 analysis into an independently verified forecast.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The third line of Qian emphasises continued effort and repeated examination of the path being followed. In 1938, while war with Japan continued, Mao Zedong published On Protracted War. The work considered the changing conditions of the conflict and proposed a way of understanding its development through stages. It was written before the future course of the war was known. The comparison is not an assertion that the essay was based on this line of the Small Image. Nor does the eventual outcome prove that every strategic claim in a contemporary text was correct. What readers can observe is an attempt to assess an unfolding situation over time, rather than turning one battle into a complete verdict. For a long-term undertaking today, the parallel question is whether assumptions are checked as circumstances change. Define the observations that would support a plan and the evidence that would require adjustment. Repeated review should clarify decisions; it must not become a ritual that substitutes slogans for information.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

01.4 — Line 4▶

01.4 — Line 4

004爻 Case ID: XCASE-H01-L4 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-01-05 | Event ID: E35 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 或躍在淵，進无咎也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「龍或躍起、或退居深淵，審時而動，沒有災咎。」《象傳》解釋：懂得審時前進，所以沒有災咎。

Historical event | Short narrative

In 1926, forces taking part in the Northern Expedition moved toward Wuchang. The city was a significant objective, but its defenders continued to control the urban position and surrounding defences. For the advancing army, reaching the vicinity did not mean that the city could immediately be occupied. The attacking force had to decide how to continue after its first attempt to take the position failed. An initial assault did not achieve the intended result. The campaign consequently developed into a longer operation that involved surrounding the city and sustaining the troops outside it. The defenders remained in place for a time, while the attackers required supplies and a continued military presence around the urban area. Civilians within the city experienced the effects of encirclement as the fighting and restrictions on normal activity continued. The operation was therefore not a single successful charge but a sequence of unsuccessful attack, maintained pressure and prolonged confrontation. The struggle continued into October 1926, when Northern Expedition forces finally took Wuchang. Possession of the city extended their political and military influence, but it followed months of operational demands and losses. The outcome did not erase the earlier setback, nor did it remove the injuries, deaths and disruption borne by combatants and residents during the siege. The wider Northern Expedition continued to face political disputes after this local military result. A factual account can identify the objective, the first unsuccessful assault, the decision to maintain the surrounding operation and the eventual change of control in October. It cannot supply imagined conversations in headquarters or personal scenes inside the besieged city that the cited material does not record. The capture of Wuchang belongs to the history of the campaign, while the conditions under which it was achieved remain part of the same story. The surviving chronology shows a change of control, not a guarantee of later political stability.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The fourth line of Qian concerns movement when the conditions for advancing are uncertain. The 1926 Northern Expedition campaign against Wuchang provides one possible historical comparison. An initial assault failed; the attackers then maintained pressure around the city, and Wuchang was taken in October after prolonged fighting. The outcome came with military losses and hardship for people inside the besieged city. Nothing in the account establishes that commanders planned their operation from this passage. The link is an interpretive reading made afterward. It is also important not to rewrite the campaign as a smooth rise from one victory to the next. The failed attack, the demands of encirclement and the city's eventual capture belong to the same sequence. A project can similarly move through several phases without any one phase guaranteeing the next. Before advancing, review available resources, the consequences of delay and the burdens carried by others. The question is not simply whether an objective was reached, but what happened on the way and what followed.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

01.5 — Line 5▶

01.5 — Line 5

005爻 Case ID: XCASE-H01-L5 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-01-06 | Event ID: E24 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 飛龍在天，大人造也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「龍飛在天，適宜拜見有德位的大人。」《象傳》解釋：有德位者已能有所作為。

Historical event | Short narrative

As Wang Mang's government collapsed, several armed and political groups competed for control of territory. Liu Xiu emerged within this unsettled environment and gradually gathered military and local support. The immediate challenge was not merely to claim a title. Any authority he established had to function in areas still affected by fighting, where communities required officials and routine administration even before the wider conflict was settled. In the year 25, Liu Xiu took the imperial title and established the Eastern Han. That political act marked a new government, but important regions remained outside his control. Military campaigns continued as the new regime extended its position. In places that came under its authority, officials had to restore records of households, manage obligations and maintain the conditions needed for agricultural production. The work of administration and the work of bringing further territory under control occurred during overlapping years. For provincial offices, an imperial declaration did not itself supply accurate population registers or the means to collect revenue. Local arrangements still had to be made, and the effects of earlier conflict had to be addressed. Rebuilding government therefore involved the less visible procedures of appointing officials, recording households and organising taxation or service as well as the more conspicuous actions of military leaders. Liu Xiu's accession was followed by a gradual consolidation across major regions. The historical sequence moves from the breakdown of the preceding government, through competition among armed groups, to a new imperial administration and its continued extension. It is misleading to compress these developments into a single day or to treat restoration of the Han name as proof that normal life resumed everywhere immediately. The account supports the broad sequence of leadership, conflict and administrative reconstruction, while the precise experiences of each locality require separate evidence. The interval between assuming the imperial title and consolidating control is essential to understanding the chronology.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The fifth line of Qian speaks of a dragon in the sky and the ability of a leading figure to act. Liu Xiu's establishment of the Eastern Han offers a retrospective historical comparison. After Wang Mang's government broke down, rival forces competed for territory. Liu Xiu took the imperial title in 25, but reunification and the restoration of local government continued afterward. Officials had to manage households, administrative duties and agricultural production while military operations remained unfinished. The example is not evidence that Liu Xiu followed this line, and the ancient imagery should not be used as a general endorsement of monarchy. It invites a narrower question: what makes authority effective after a public appointment or political declaration? An office must still process information, allocate responsibility and sustain ordinary work. For a new manager or institution, a title may signal a beginning, but it does not complete the practical changes. Examine who can carry out decisions, what records are needed and which communities bear the cost of transition.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

01.6 — Line 6▶

01.6 — Line 6

006爻 Case ID: XCASE-H01-L6 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-01-07 | Event ID: E34 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 亢龍有悔，盈不可久也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「龍升得過高，將有悔恨。」《象傳》解釋：任何事物過度滿盈，都不可能長久。

Historical event | Short narrative

Fu Jian ruled Former Qin at a time when it controlled extensive territory in northern China. That territorial strength allowed the government to assemble a large force for a campaign against Eastern Jin in the south. Preparing the expedition, however, required more than counting soldiers. Forces drawn from different areas had to travel together, receive supplies and remain subject to workable command arrangements. Eastern Jin was also preparing to resist the advance. In 383, the opposing armies confronted one another near the Fei River. The campaign did not produce the result sought by Former Qin. Eastern Jin forces counterattacked, and the Former Qin army suffered a major defeat and collapse of its advance. The military outcome exposed the difference between possessing extensive resources and being able to keep a complex army coordinated under battlefield pressure. Defeat had consequences beyond the immediate fighting. Forces and territories that had previously remained within the Former Qin political structure began to reassess their positions as central control weakened. Fragmentation within the regime became more apparent, and the campaign failed to establish the southern dominance Fu Jian had attempted to achieve. The effects were therefore military and political: an invasion was halted, while the authority holding a wider state together suffered a major setback. Later historical accounts contain memorable battlefield scenes and estimates of troop numbers, but these should not be treated as a perfectly verified operational record. The basic progression is clearer: a northern government mobilised for a major expedition; its forces advanced toward Eastern Jin; they were defeated in 383; and the regime faced increasing instability afterward. That sequence does not require invented orders, speeches or the assumption that one personal trait was solely responsible for the outcome. Organisation, command, the opposing forces and the political structure all belong to the setting in which the campaign occurred.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The upper line of Qian warns that excessive height or fullness cannot last without consequence. Fu Jian's southern campaign is an illustrative comparison. Former Qin controlled a wide northern territory and mobilised major forces against Eastern Jin. In 383 the expedition was defeated near the Fei River. The failure was followed by growing instability within Former Qin's wider political structure. A retrospective comparison must not become a claim of prophecy. No evidence here shows that Fu Jian used this Small Image commentary when planning his invasion. It is equally misleading to explain a complex defeat with a single word such as pride. Mobilisation, supplies, command across diverse forces, Eastern Jin resistance and subsequent political fragmentation all belong to the account. In a modern organisation, rapid growth or extensive resources may create demands that existing procedures cannot meet. Ask whether systems can sustain the scale of an undertaking, and whether contrary evidence is reaching decision-makers. The purpose of the comparison is to examine limits, not to declare any outcome inevitable.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

02.1 — Line 1▶

02.1 — Line 1

007爻 Case ID: XCASE-H02-L1 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-02-02 | Event ID: E55 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 履霜堅冰，陰始凝也。馴致其道，至堅冰也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「腳踏秋霜，便知堅冰將至；微小跡象預示後勢。」《象傳》解釋：陰始凝。「馴致它的道」《象傳》解釋：至堅冰。

Historical event | Short narrative

During the later years of Emperor Xuanzong’s Tang reign, the court governed a large territory and presided over an era remembered for its prosperity. Responsibility for defense, however, rested increasingly with powerful regional military commands. Their commanders controlled troops and local resources while the central court attempted to maintain authority over appointments and major decisions. An Lushan held important frontier commands. The concentration of military forces outside the capital developed over time, alongside disputes and growing tension between regional and central authorities. Prosperity at the imperial center did not remove those administrative and military differences. In 755, An Lushan raised an army against the Tang government. The rebellion changed the situation from a prolonged problem of command and allegiance into open warfare. Rebel forces advanced through territory that had belonged to the imperial administration. Tang officials had to organize military resistance while the court confronted the consequences of losing control of key approaches to the capital. Emperor Xuanzong subsequently left Chang’an. The departure was one visible consequence of a much broader conflict, not the first sign that the system had come under strain. The fighting continued for years. Military operations displaced people, interfered with farming and revenue collection, and altered relations between the central government and regional commanders. Local officials and armies had to handle immediate supplies and security as fighting spread. The settlement of one battlefield did not restore the earlier distribution of authority. Later histories describe both the preceding prosperity and the political difficulties that accumulated during it. The sequence supported by the source is therefore gradual concentration of military power, the uprising in 755, the court’s withdrawal, and a prolonged conflict whose effects extended into Tang administration. The text does not establish that any single warning, official, or incident by itself made the rebellion inevitable. The supplied account distinguishes this long-term deterioration from a single dramatic episode at the imperial palace.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The first line of the Kun hexagram’s *Small Image* describes frost as the early stage of a process that can eventually produce hard ice. The account of the late Tang provides a retrospective comparison: regional commanders accumulated military resources while the court continued to preside over a prosperous realm. In 755, the tensions became an armed rebellion, followed by years of war and administrative disruption. For a modern institution, the practical question is not whether a disaster can be predicted from an image. It is whether changes in authority, accountability, and access to reliable information are being observed while there is still time to respond. A successful quarter or a crowded calendar can coexist with unresolved problems in decision-making. Record who controls critical resources, who can challenge a decision, and which problems are repeatedly postponed. This is an interpretive analogy, not evidence that Tang rulers used this passage to diagnose the frontier system. Nor should the frost image replace historical analysis of the rebellion’s political and military causes.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

02.2 — Line 2▶

02.2 — Line 2

008爻 Case ID: XCASE-H02-L2 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-02-03 | Event ID: E41 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 六二之動，直以方也。不習无不利，地道光也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「六二的動」《象傳》解釋：直以方。「正直、端方、廣大，不經刻意造作也無所不利。」《象傳》解釋：地道光。

Historical event | Short narrative

In the early Western Han, farming formed a major part of ordinary livelihoods and government revenue. Households cultivated land and used their harvests both for family needs and to meet obligations to the state. The court, in turn, relied on collections such as the land tax to finance its responsibilities. Any decision to reduce a tax on agricultural production therefore affected two sides of the same arrangement: what cultivating households were required to surrender and what officials could collect for the treasury. According to the *Records of the Grand Historian*, in the thirteenth year of Emperor Wen’s reign the ruler ordered the removal of the land tax. This was a definite administrative measure, not simply a declaration of sympathy toward farmers. Its implementation required officials responsible for assessment and collection to change what they demanded. Cultivating households no longer faced that particular land-tax charge under the order. The resulting change in state revenue had to be understood alongside the court’s other sources of income and expenditure. The consequences were narrower than the claim that taxation had ended altogether. Other taxes, labor obligations, and differences in landholding remained relevant to the lives of households. A family’s benefit depended on its particular situation, and the surviving record does not give an audited account for each farm. The episode does, however, provide a discernible chain of events: a government dependent on agricultural production considered the burden placed on cultivators, the emperor issued a removal order, and the administration had to adjust collection practices. This choice belongs to a longer history of attempts to restore production and civil life in the early Han. Neither the order nor the chronicle proves that conditions became identical for every farmer. No undocumented conversations with farmers or precise household income changes have been added here. This tax measure can be identified without assuming that every other fiscal demand disappeared at the same time.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The Kun line speaks of direct and grounded action. Emperor Wen’s abolition of the land tax offers a historical comparison because the decision changed a specific obligation rather than relying only on a general statement about helping the population. The historical record identifies a measure and a time; it does not provide the complete experience of every agricultural household. When leaders announce that a policy will reduce a burden, readers can ask what will actually change on the next payment date. Which fee disappears? Who will update the records? Which other obligations remain? What resources will fund the services that continue? These questions help separate an announced objective from the administrative work needed to carry it out. The comparison does not suggest that all taxes are harmful or that eliminating a single tax resolves unequal access to land. It also does not imply that Emperor Wen acted under the guidance of the *Small Image*. The useful distinction is between public language and a change people can verify in their own transactions.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

02.3 — Line 3▶

02.3 — Line 3

009爻 Case ID: XCASE-H02-L3 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-02-04 | Event ID: E27 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 含章可貞，以時發也。或從王事，知光大也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「含藏美德而守正；若參與君王之事，不居功，仍能善終。」《象傳》解釋：以時發。「含藏美德而守正；若參與君王之事，不居功，仍能善終。」《象傳》解釋：知光大。

Historical event | Short narrative

During the struggle between Liu Bang and Xiang Yu, armies repeatedly moved and fought across different regions. Each campaign consumed food and required additional personnel. A force could win a battle and still be unable to continue if the territory behind it stopped producing supplies or maintaining records. The Guanzhong region came under Liu Bang’s control and could serve as an administrative base. Maintaining that base required more than the presence of troops: officials had to know the local population, organize material resources, and keep the machinery of government functioning. Xiao He remained largely in Guanzhong while Liu Bang’s armies conducted operations elsewhere. Historical accounts, including the *Book of Han*, connect Xiao He’s responsibilities with the management of population records, grain, and the replenishment of soldiers. Personnel had to be identified and made available; food had to be gathered and moved toward the forces that needed it. These processes were repeated as campaigns continued. Xiao He’s work took place away from many of the battles, but it was connected to them through the continuing demand for people and provisions. The fighting did not conclude after a single delivery. New campaigns created further demands on the same region, while local government had to remain capable of serving its residents and collecting resources. The histories later recognized these administrative efforts as an important part of Liu Bang’s ability to sustain a prolonged contest. That recognition should not erase the labor of unnamed farmers, transport workers, and local officials. The documented sequence is a wartime supply requirement, the continued management of Guanzhong under Xiao He, and repeated support for armies still in the field. It is not a detailed record of every shipment, nor does it show that the ultimate outcome depended on one administrator alone. The precise contributions of individual couriers, cultivators, and officials cannot be reconstructed from the available summary.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The third line of Kun can be read as a reminder that contributing to a shared undertaking does not always mean appearing at the front of it. Xiao He’s role during the Chu–Han struggle offers a historical analogy. While military commanders fought, he managed population records, personnel, and supplies in Guanzhong. The value of that work lay in its continued connection to the needs of the armies. In a present-day organization, visible achievements often depend on less visible routines: maintaining reliable data, paying workers, transporting materials, and supporting people who must deliver the final service. A project review should identify those tasks rather than naming only the public-facing leader. Ask which recurring work would cause the next stage to stop if it were neglected. Then provide the resources and recognition needed to sustain it. This is a later reading of the hexagram, not evidence that Xiao He quoted its *Small Image*. Historical recognition of his role also does not justify attributing all military outcomes to him or overlooking the burden of wartime requisitions.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

02.4 — Line 4▶

02.4 — Line 4

010爻 Case ID: XCASE-H02-L4 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-02-05 | Event ID: E36 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 括囊无咎，慎不害也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「束緊袋口，謹言慎行，沒有災咎，也沒有聲譽。」《象傳》解釋：慎不害。

Historical event | Short narrative

Near the end of the Shang period, the leaders of the Zhou polity operated under a more powerful royal court. In later historical writing, relations between Xibo Chang, traditionally identified with King Wen of Zhou, and the Shang ruler are depicted as tense. The *Records of the Grand Historian* recounts that the Shang king detained Xibo Chang at Youli. This placed a leading figure of the Zhou polity under the control of a stronger political authority, while those connected to him still had to maintain the affairs of their community. The detention interrupted Xibo Chang’s ability to carry on his usual political activities. The historical tradition says that his followers sought means to secure his release. Their work took place while the outcome was uncertain: they could continue managing relationships and appeal to the Shang ruler, but they could not simply order the prisoner freed. The account eventually records Xibo Chang’s release. The narrative therefore has a limited but clear progression from tension between rulers, to confinement at Youli, to efforts by followers, and finally to his return from captivity. Release did not mean that the Zhou immediately governed the wider realm. Political developments associated with the Zhou unfolded afterward and involved other actors and events. The surviving account was compiled long after the period described, and the exact dates and private exchanges cannot be checked in the same manner as modern administrative records. Later traditions link imprisonment with the composition of the *Changes*, but that association should not be inserted into this particular episode as a verified daily activity. The account allows us to say that he was detained, his followers worked for his release, and he eventually resumed life outside confinement. It does not provide evidence of each conversation, personal calculation, or protective strategy used during captivity. Later victory should never be projected backward as certainty during the period of captivity.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Kun’s fourth-line commentary relates restraint to avoiding further harm. The traditional account of Xibo Chang’s detention at Youli may be compared with a situation in which political authority is unequal and the person detained cannot freely act. His followers sought release while the Zhou polity continued to face the demands of survival and governance. For modern readers, the lesson is not that silence is always the proper response to an unjust situation. It is to distinguish what the evidence actually shows from the tactics we might imagine someone used. When a person faces a powerful institution, reliable communication, access to appropriate assistance, and a clear record of events matter. Decisions also need to account for the safety of others affected by the dispute. This is an analogy between a *Small Image* passage and a much later account of a political detention. It does not establish that Xibo Chang deliberately followed this text, and it should not turn his involuntary confinement into a story of voluntary withdrawal or guaranteed eventual triumph.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

02.5 — Line 5▶

02.5 — Line 5

011爻 Case ID: XCASE-H02-L5 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-02-06 | Event ID: E15 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 黃裳元吉，文在中也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「穿黃色下裳，居中守分，大吉。」《象傳》解釋：文在中。

Historical event | Short narrative

During the establishment of the Eastern Han, Liu Xiu depended on commanders who led troops in different campaigns. Those commanders accumulated military achievements while a new political order was taking shape. Their work gave rise to questions of appointment, reputation, and recognition. When commanders gathered, discussion of their individual exploits could become part of the way they measured standing among peers. Feng Yi was one of the commanders serving in those campaigns, not a spectator detached from military responsibilities. The *Book of the Later Han* reports that when other generals assembled to discuss their achievements, Feng Yi commonly withdrew to sit beneath a tree rather than participate in competing claims. This habit became associated with the nickname “General of the Great Tree.” The account remembers a particular kind of behavior in a recognizable setting: colleagues talking about military merit while a fellow commander chose not to join the competition. The nickname emerged from that reported practice rather than from a formal military rank named after a tree. Feng Yi continued to serve as a commander. Avoiding argument over credit did not mean that he refused every appointment, abandoned operations, or denied that he had made a contribution. His responsibilities continued alongside the reputation recorded by the historian. The biographical source offers a selected portrait and does not provide transcripts of every gathering or a complete comparison of individual battle records. It would therefore be misleading to invent conversations in which colleagues praised him, or to claim certainty about what he privately thought. The supported chronology is participation in the wars of state formation, gatherings where commanders discussed merit, Feng Yi’s reported withdrawal to the tree, and the later preservation of his nickname. His long-standing reputation and actual service must be read together rather than reduced to one gesture. His example supplies a biographical scene, rather than a comprehensive account of military service.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The *Small Image* describes the value of something cultivated within rather than merely displayed outside. Feng Yi’s biography offers a retrospective comparison. The commander reportedly stepped away when colleagues argued about their achievements, yet he continued his military duties. His restraint became part of the way later historians remembered him. In a workplace, this does not mean that people should conceal their contributions or avoid discussing fair recognition. Good records distinguish personal responsibility from work completed jointly. A leader can describe results accurately while also naming the people and systems that made them possible. Equally, a quiet colleague should not be assumed to have done less simply because that person speaks less during a review. This is not evidence that Feng Yi used the Kun line as a rule for conduct. The biography is a selected and partly admiring portrait, not an independent survey of every commander’s motives. The useful modern question is how achievement can be recognized without allowing claims of prestige to crowd out the work itself.

Small Image original: 龍戰于野，其道窮也。

Historical event | Short narrative

During the first period of cooperation between the Chinese Nationalist Party and the Chinese Communist Party, members of both organizations took part in political and military activity associated with the Northern Expedition. Their shared participation did not remove differences over control of armed forces, authority in cities, or the organization of workers and farmers. As the expedition advanced, those questions became more immediate. Military successes altered who held influence in newly controlled places, and each organization had its own positions on how power should be exercised. In 1927, the disagreements developed into a political rupture. In Shanghai, the Nationalist purge of Communist and associated political groups involved serious violence. Separate political developments in Wuhan also led to a break with the Communists. The Shanghai and Wuhan episodes were not a single event occurring at exactly the same place or time, and their decision-makers and victims should not be treated as interchangeable. They were connected parts of the wider collapse of cooperation. Political affiliation and access to weapons became matters of immediate danger for people who had previously operated within parts of the same alliance. The consequences extended beyond a change in party announcements. People faced detention, flight, and death; organizations altered their political and military arrangements; and the two parties entered a prolonged period of armed confrontation. The earlier partnership did not simply return once the immediate actions were over. The sequence supported by the source is cooperation during the Northern Expedition, growing differences over authority and mobilization, violent and political ruptures in 1927, and the development of longer conflict afterward. The narrative does not reduce responsibility to a single phrase such as “a disagreement,” nor does it equate all participants’ actions. Each location and phase requires its own historical evidence, and no private dialogue has been added to connect events that the available record already places in sequence.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Kun’s final line portrays a confrontation after a relationship has reached its limit. The breakdown of the first Nationalist–Communist United Front in 1927 offers an interpretive analogy, but its history must remain specific. Political and military disagreements accumulated during a period of cooperation; separate actions in Shanghai and Wuhan contributed to the rupture; and political violence accompanied the transition to prolonged conflict. A modern partnership should not be judged simply by whether its members once signed a common declaration. Who controls resources? How are disagreements resolved? Do people who criticize the leadership have safe channels for doing so? Are members protected if cooperation ends? Such questions matter before a conflict becomes irreversible. They also help avoid romanticizing confrontation as an unavoidable final act. The hexagram does not explain or predict the violence of 1927. This comparison was created afterward, and no evidence in the supplied text shows that political actors chose their actions because of the *Small Image*. A struggle over succession in the state of Jin forced Chong’er to leave the country where he had once belonged to the ruling family. Exile deprived him of the offices and resources that someone of his standing might otherwise have expected to use. He travelled among other states with followers whose continued presence mattered to his prospects. At each destination the party depended on its hosts for reception and practical support. Being related to a ruling house did not itself compel another court to provide shelter or assistance. The reception changed from place to place. Some rulers provided help, while others treated the exiles with less consideration. Chong’er and his companions had to continue their travels despite these differences. The surviving account presents a prolonged period of movement and dependence rather than an uninterrupted advance toward power. A court that agreed to receive the party could provide a temporary place to remain, but hospitality was not the same thing as an army willing to restore him to Jin. That return followed years of displacement, changing receptions, and relationships maintained across state boundaries. It was not an outcome guaranteed when he first departed. His followers' continued participation and Qin's eventual intervention formed part of the practical chain of events, together with the situation inside Jin. The available narrative does not allow a precise reconstruction of every conversation or calculation made during the journey. What it does establish is the sequence: a succession dispute led to departure; the exile endured uncertain reception in several courts; outside assistance later enabled his return. His eventual accession gives the journey an identifiable ending without making every earlier stop a step in a predetermined plan.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The first line of Zhun speaks of hesitation at the beginning while maintaining a proper direction, and of gaining people through consideration rather than rank alone. Chong’er’s exile offers a comparison. His former status could not supply food, shelter, or armed support after he left Jin. He and his companions depended on relationships that had to be sustained through years of uncertain travel. For someone starting a difficult public project, the practical lesson is to identify the people whose cooperation makes the next step possible. Who supplies the necessary resources? Who remains involved when progress is slower than expected? Who has the authority to help when conditions change? A title or an ambitious announcement cannot answer those questions. This is a later interpretive analogy, not evidence that Chong’er used this passage to plan his travels. Small Image original: 六二之難，乘剛也。十年乃字，反常也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「六二的難」《象傳》解釋：乘剛。「進退艱難，騎馬者徘徊不前；來者不是盜賊而是求婚者。女子守正不嫁，十年後才成婚。」《象傳》解釋：反常。

Historical event | Short narrative

In 1906, the Qing court announced that it would prepare for constitutional government. The declaration came amid demands to change political institutions and to establish clearer limits on authority. Supporters of reform wanted an opportunity for political participation, while the imperial household intended to retain a leading role in the new arrangements. Their expectations differed not only over the final design but also over how quickly meaningful powers would be transferred. The initial announcement created a public promise whose significance would be tested by later decisions. The government subsequently published a program of preparatory steps and introduced consultative institutions, including provincial assemblies and a central advisory body. These institutions provided places in which some supporters of constitutional reform could participate in formal discussion. Yet the existence of a meeting body did not settle how much power it could exercise. Participants could compare newly established procedures with earlier promises, while the court continued to determine important parts of the timetable and the imperial prerogatives. Disagreements over the pace of reform and the distribution of authority therefore persisted across several years rather than appearing at a single meeting. In 1911, the composition of the new cabinet added to existing dissatisfaction. Critics questioned whether the personnel arrangements represented the promised redistribution of authority. Confidence among some constitutional supporters weakened as revolutionary activity and political changes in the provinces intensified. The Qing political order subsequently collapsed amid developments wider than the cabinet issue itself. The record supports a chronological account of an announcement, a staged program, the creation of institutions, and a later loss of confidence. It does not justify reducing the dynasty's end to one appointment or assuming that all reform supporters held identical views. The central difficulty was the distance between what the constitutional project had appeared to promise and what its institutional arrangements actually allowed. That distance became more visible as the promised preparations advanced.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Zhun’s second line describes an extended difficulty before an anticipated arrangement becomes possible. The Qing court’s constitutional preparations supply a historical comparison: an announcement in 1906 was followed by new consultative institutions, but disputes about real authority and the timetable continued. By 1911, personnel choices further damaged confidence among some people who had supported reform. In a modern organization, a transition plan should specify what changes at each stage. Does a new committee have decision-making power or only permission to advise? Who can revise the schedule? How will participants know whether earlier promises have been fulfilled? These questions are more informative than the number of meetings held or the new titles given to an office. This analogy does not treat the line’s reference to ten years as a prediction of Qing history. Constitutional reform, revolutionary mobilization, and the end of imperial government involved several causes and actors. The useful comparison concerns a recurring practical problem: when announced participation and actual authority remain far apart, the passage of time alone does not restore trust.

By the early 380s, Fu Jian ruled the Former Qin state, whose authority extended over a large part of northern China. He decided to mount a major campaign against Eastern Jin in the south. Control of extensive territory made it possible to assemble substantial forces, but gathering soldiers from different regions did not make them a single coordinated body. Such an expedition depended on transport, supplies, command, and the willingness of its constituent forces to keep acting together. Eastern Jin, meanwhile, organized resistance in the region of the Huai River. The armies met in the Fei River area in 383. Accounts describe the southern campaign as a major undertaking, yet the size of the reported forces and dramatic battlefield speeches require caution. What the sources consistently establish is the confrontation, the Eastern Jin counterattack, and the rout of Former Qin troops. The northern army's numerical advantage, whatever its precise size, did not secure effective coordination during the battle. Once its formation broke down, the invading force could no longer accomplish the campaign's intended result. Retreat also placed demands on a coalition whose units had been drawn from different parts of the state. The defeat had consequences beyond the immediate battlefield. Former Qin had united various regional and political forces under one ruling structure, and the loss at Fei River weakened that structure. Divisions became more evident as the regime's control deteriorated. The sequence therefore runs from the decision to invade and the mobilization of a large army, through defeat on the southern front, to subsequent political fragmentation. It cannot be explained adequately by attributing everything to a ruler's confidence or to a single maneuver described in a later narrative. Logistics, command relationships, the opposing army's action, and the political composition of Former Qin all belong to the historical context. The sources do not establish that Fu Jian consulted Zhun or that this text influenced the expedition.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Zhun’s third line warns against pursuing a goal without reliable guidance. Fu Jian’s campaign against Eastern Jin can be read beside it. Former Qin could mobilize extensive forces, yet the army was defeated at Fei River in 383, and the political structure supporting the expedition weakened afterward. Scale did not remove the need for coordination, supplies, and accurate judgments about the opponent. Before committing an organization to a difficult objective, distinguish what is known from what is merely assumed. Are several teams able to act under compatible instructions? Can the available supply system support the plan? Is there a practical condition under which the project should be suspended? The point is not to avoid every uncertain undertaking, but to decide what evidence is required before increasing exposure. This is a retrospective analogy, not an assertion that Fu Jian ignored a particular ancient warning. The defeat had multiple military and political causes, and reported troop figures must be treated critically. The line offers a question for judgment; it does not deliver a historical verdict or predict defeat.

When Cao Cao moved south, conditions in Jing Province changed rapidly. Liu Bei could no longer rely on his earlier position, while Sun Quan had to consider the defense of his territory along the Yangtze. Each side possessed its own political following and military obligations. Neither could assume that the other would automatically accept an alliance, although both faced pressure from the same advancing northern force. The situation made contact and negotiation increasingly important. Representatives including Lu Su and Zhuge Liang took part in the exchanges that helped establish cooperation between Sun Quan and Liu Bei. Their discussions had to bridge separate chains of command and interests. An agreement to resist Cao Cao did not abolish either side's need to control its own forces. It provided a basis for coordinated action against an immediate threat. The allied forces subsequently confronted Cao Cao's army in the Red Cliffs campaign and achieved a military result that altered the course of his southern advance. That outcome followed contacts, negotiation, and the practical organization of joint resistance, not simply a declaration of friendship. After the battle, the two partners continued to administer their own territories and consider their own strategic interests. The question of Jing Province remained an important source of later disagreement. Their wartime cooperation therefore did not produce a permanent identity of aims. It is possible to describe a clear sequence: Cao Cao's advance put both parties under pressure; envoys explored an alliance; the partners acted together at Red Cliffs; and disputes over territorial interests continued after the immediate confrontation. The surviving narratives record negotiations and actions, but their dramatic dialogue should not be treated as a verbatim transcript of every meeting. Nor should the later disputes be projected backward as proof that cooperation was insincere from the beginning. The alliance had a concrete wartime purpose, and the parties had to reassess their relationship once that circumstance changed.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Zhun’s fourth line is unusually direct: when help is needed, seeking it can show clear judgment. Sun Quan and Liu Bei faced Cao Cao's advance from different positions. Their representatives negotiated a shared response, and their forces acted together in the Red Cliffs campaign. Cooperation came from identifying an overlapping need, not from pretending the two sides had identical long-term interests. When a project exceeds one team’s capacity, begin by stating precisely what help is required. What can each partner contribute? Who retains decision-making authority? 017爻 Case ID: XCASE-H03-L5 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-03-06 | Event ID: E42 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 屯其膏，施未光也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「恩澤難以施展；小事守正可吉，大事若仍僵守則凶。」《象傳》解釋：施作用尚未充分顯明。

Historical event | Short narrative

In Northern Song China, farming households often needed resources before the harvest brought income. Borrowing during that interval could create difficulties, particularly when private loans carried demanding terms. Wang Anshi's reform program introduced the Green Sprouts policy, under which government offices would provide seasonal loans. The policy was presented partly as a means of offering credit when farm households needed working funds, while also changing the government's financial arrangements. Its intended effect could only be tested after officials began administering the loans. Implementation brought decisions that could not be settled by the name of the law. Local officials controlled distribution, assessment, and collection. Households faced the amount borrowed, the interest due, and the timing of repayment. In places where officials pressed households to accept loans or used lending targets to judge performance, a program intended to relieve a shortage of funds could itself add an obligation. The problem was not merely whether money left a government office. It also involved whether the recipient had wanted the loan and could repay it under the circumstances of the coming harvest. Disagreement over the policy appeared in court debates and accounts of local administration. Supporters stressed the purpose of making credit available and improving financial administration. Critics raised questions about coercion, collection practices, and burdens on households. The records thus allow a sequence to be traced: an agricultural credit problem prompted a policy design; officials administered loans and collected repayments; controversy developed about what borrowers actually experienced. They do not establish that every locality followed one pattern or that the policy helped or harmed every household equally. Nor is the sum disbursed a reliable measure of its benefit. The distinction between the reform's stated intention and its varying execution remains central to understanding why the Green Sprouts law became the subject of prolonged disagreement.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Zhun’s fifth line refers to resources whose benefits have not fully spread. The Green Sprouts policy under Wang Anshi offers a useful historical comparison. Seasonal government loans were meant partly to provide farmers with funds before harvest, yet administration, interest, repayment, and reports of compulsory lending all became points of dispute. An amount recorded as assistance did not necessarily mean that a household experienced it as help. Before offering a loan, subsidy, or organizational resource, ask whether the recipient actually needs that form of support. Can participation be refused? What obligations follow later? Who is responsible for checking whether the assistance solved the original difficulty? The answers matter as much as the amount of money provided. This is an editorial interpretation, not evidence that the reformers used this line to design their policy. Historians disagree about outcomes across places and periods; different experiences should not be flattened into one verdict. The practical message is to check delivery and consequences rather than treat good intentions or impressive distribution totals as proof of success.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

Small Image original: 泣血漣如，何可長也。

Historical event | Short narrative

During the early phase of the Long March, the Central Red Army moved toward the Xiang River while facing forces attempting to block its route and others pursuing from behind. Crossing was not a single movement by a small body of soldiers. Units had to pass through a constrained area while moving equipment, supplies, and personnel accompanying the force. The order in which formations crossed mattered, because some had to maintain access to the route while others moved onward. The presence of opposing troops turned the river area into a major military obstacle. Fighting around the crossing caused severe casualties and organizational losses. Some units were engaged in protecting the movement of others, and the pressure on the route affected the force's ability to maintain its earlier organization. The losses cannot be adequately described by a neat figure alone. Different accounts measure personnel reductions over different dates or include different groups, so numbers for the whole early Long March should not automatically be assigned to the Xiang River fighting. What is clear is that the operation imposed a heavy human and military cost while part of the force continued across the river. Those who survived proceeded with the march, but crossing the water did not undo the deaths and disruption that had occurred. The experience was followed by examination and changes in the Red Army's direction and command arrangements as the wider campaign developed. Those subsequent developments must be distinguished from the battle itself. The story can be told without inventing speeches on the riverbank or attributing private emotions to people whose words were not recorded: a moving army approached a defended crossing; severe fighting took place while its formations attempted to pass; surviving units continued, having lost personnel and organizational capacity. Any interpretation of command decisions should be tied to the relevant sources and dates. The river crossing was a concrete military event with lasting consequences, not a symbolic episode whose losses can be turned into a satisfying ending.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Zhun’s final line asks how long a condition of overwhelming distress can continue. The Xiang River fighting during the early Long March gives this question historical weight. The Central Red Army attempted a difficult crossing while being blocked and pursued, and it suffered serious human and organizational losses. Some formations continued onward, but their survival did not erase the cost. For a present-day institution, the comparison is about recognizing damage before it becomes the only normal condition. Which commitments can no longer be met with available people and supplies? Which reports indicate that current methods are failing? Who can review the situation without requiring those exposed to danger to defend an earlier decision? Changing a plan may be necessary even when substantial effort has already been invested. The analogy is not a celebration of suffering or a claim that the commentary predicted a battle. Historical estimates of losses differ in scope and require careful attribution. The source case should retain that uncertainty and the experiences of those harmed, rather than converting the crossing into a simplified lesson about endurance.

Historical event | Short narrative

As Qin rule collapsed, competing armies advanced toward Guanzhong, the region that had housed the Qin political center. Liu Bang reached the area with troops whose arrival introduced another change of authority. For residents, the question was not only which commander had entered the region. They also had to learn whether the occupying forces would continue Qin penalties, impose different demands, or interfere with ordinary life. Qin law had acquired a reputation for severity, and uncertainty about the new army's conduct could hinder any attempt to administer the territory. After entering Guanzhong, Liu Bang gathered local elders and announced three basic legal provisions, a measure later remembered as the Agreement of Three Articles. The declaration replaced a complicated public impression of punitive government with a short statement residents could understand. Announcing the provisions was a political act directed at local cooperation. It also imposed a practical obligation on the new authorities: officials and soldiers would have to act consistently with the announced rules. The measure did not remove the presence of armed men or the competition among commanders. It provided a statement against which the conduct of those in power could be assessed. The immediate aftermath remained uncertain. Other military forces, including Xiang Yu's, continued to contest control of territory after the Qin collapse. Liu Bang's arrival and his legal announcement did not make him ruler of the whole country. In the following struggle, promises to local residents were only one part of a larger contest involving troops, supplies and political alliances. The historical sequence is therefore an advance into Guanzhong, a public decision about law and local order, and continued competition for authority. The surviving accounts do not establish that everyone responded alike or that every subsequent action fulfilled the pledge. They do preserve the significance of making administrative rules intelligible while power was changing hands.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The first line of Meng discusses discipline at the beginning of instruction. Liu Bang's announcement of three legal provisions after entering Guanzhong offers a comparison: before people could cooperate with a new administration, they needed to know what rules would apply. The historical event involved military occupation and political competition, not a modern classroom or workplace training program. For a new team, clarity should precede punishment. Explain what conduct is required, who may make decisions, and how mistakes will be addressed. A rule that no one can understand is difficult to follow fairly. Once the rule is announced, the person in authority must also observe it. That is how a written expectation becomes part of daily practice. This is a retrospective reading of the Small Image, not evidence that Liu Bang quoted it. The ancient passage refers to penal discipline, but it should not be treated as approval of harsh punishment today. The useful comparison is limited to clear procedures, consistent enforcement and accountability for people exercising power.

Small Image original: 勿用取女，行不順也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「不宜娶這樣的女子：她見到有財勢的男子便失去自持，沒有利益。」《象傳》解釋：行不順。

Historical event | Short narrative

After the founding of the Republic of China, Yuan Shikai occupied a central position in national government. His formal authority did not settle relations with provincial leaders, military commanders and political groups. The republican framework created expectations about the form of government, while regional forces retained resources and influence of their own. Any attempt to change that framework would require acceptance beyond the offices closest to Yuan. In 1915 Yuan moved toward a restoration of monarchy and the assumption of an imperial title. Supporters promoted the change, but public advocacy from his circle did not mean that provincial authorities and armed forces had agreed to the new political arrangement. The proposal directly altered the republican structure under which Yuan had acquired power. Opposition developed across political and regional networks. The movement commonly called the National Protection campaign challenged the imperial project, and military resistance followed the political break. As resistance widened, some figures and forces that had previously cooperated with Yuan ceased to support his plans. Opposition was not merely a disagreement about ceremonial names. It affected the ability of the central government to secure orders, retain regional allegiance and mobilize troops. What began as a proposed change in constitutional status turned into a conflict over who would exercise governing authority. Yuan cancelled the imperial system in 1916. That reversal was a concrete political outcome, but it did not immediately resolve the fragmentation of national power or the disagreements that had emerged during the crisis. The sequence is thus a republic with unresolved regional tensions, an attempted imperial change, resistance that included armed conflict, and the abandonment of the new monarchy. The surviving record supports those public developments. It does not require invented statements of private ambition from participants or a claim that every supporter changed position for the same reason. The case illustrates a political reversal whose consequences continued beyond the formal cancellation of the imperial title.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Meng's third line uses an ancient marriage image to question a course that cannot proceed properly. Yuan Shikai's attempt to establish an empire after a republic had been founded provides one possible political comparison. His 1915 initiative produced opposition and armed resistance, and the imperial system was cancelled in 1916. Public acclaim from supporters did not establish agreement among the authorities whose cooperation was needed. Before accepting a powerful role or announcing a major organizational change, ask whose consent is necessary and which existing commitments the change would disturb. A proposal may look complete within a leadership circle while its implementation depends on people outside that circle. Their ability to object is a material condition, not merely a public-relations problem. This is a retrospective analogy; no source shows Yuan using this Small Image as a guide. The gendered marriage wording belongs to the ancient passage and should not be repurposed to criticize women. Nor should a complex political collapse be explained through a single moral flaw. The relevant question is whether a decision has an adequate, openly tested basis for support.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

022爻 Case ID: XCASE-H04-L4 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-04-05 | Event ID: E62 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 困蒙之吝，獨遠實也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「困蒙的吝」《象傳》解釋：獨自遠離實際情況。

Historical event | Short narrative

In 1900, the Qing court confronted a rapidly changing crisis involving the Boxer movement, foreign powers and disputes within its own government. Armed intervention by foreign states combined with domestic mobilization to produce an increasingly dangerous situation around Beijing. The court had to decide how to respond to foreign forces and to the Boxers, while senior officials in different regions assessed the risks to their own populations and administrations. These assessments did not produce a single uniform policy. As the confrontation intensified, the Qing government issued an edict of war against foreign powers. Its declaration did not ensure that officials across the empire could carry out a common military plan. Some southeastern authorities pursued arrangements subsequently described as Southeastern Mutual Protection, reflecting their departure from the direction taken at the center. Foreign allied forces advanced on Beijing as fighting grew. The conflict cannot be reduced to an internal Chinese argument: armed foreign intervention was an integral part of its escalation. The allied forces entered Beijing, and the imperial court fled the capital. In 1901, the Qing government signed the Boxer Protocol, accepting major political and financial consequences. The crisis affected residents, local officials and national finances, not only decision makers at court. The sequence moved from competing responses to the Boxer movement and foreign military pressure, through a declaration of war and divergent provincial responses, to the occupation of Beijing and a treaty imposed after the fighting. Different actors made decisions at different moments, and the regional approaches did not all match central instructions. The record does not justify treating the Boxers as a single group with identical intentions or asserting that a particular private conversation determined every stage of the conflict. It also does not support attributing the war solely to the Qing court while omitting the actions of invading foreign armies. What can be traced is a failure to maintain a workable connection between central decisions, provincial assessments, actual military capabilities and rapidly changing conditions on the ground.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Meng's fourth line warns about ignorance sustained by distance from reality. The crisis of 1900 presents a political setting in which the Qing court, provincial officials and foreign military powers acted under sharply different assessments. The declaration of war, southeastern regional arrangements, the fall of Beijing and the subsequent Boxer Protocol show that decisions at the center did not create unified action across the country. In any difficult organization, a senior announcement should be tested against conditions at the places where it must be implemented. Which teams have the people and resources to act? What evidence contradicts the official assumptions? Who can safely report that a plan is failing? A decision becomes especially dangerous when disagreement is interpreted only as disloyalty. The historical analogy has limits. The event involved foreign armed intervention as well as internal Qing failures; its costs cannot be assigned to one actor alone. The source does not document a quotation of this Small Image by the Qing authorities. The passage is useful as a prompt to examine evidence, not as proof that a classical sentence explains the entire crisis.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

023爻 Case ID: XCASE-H04-L5 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-04-06 | Event ID: E04 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 童蒙之吉，順以巽也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「童蒙的吉」《象傳》解釋：順以巽。

Historical event | Short narrative

Lü Meng had already become an active officer in Sun Quan's service when questions of further education arose. His duties involved military affairs, leaving little time for extended study. Sun Quan nevertheless considered historical reading useful to an officer who needed to understand political events and other commanders' choices. The concern was not that Lü Meng lacked battlefield experience. Rather, service required forms of knowledge beyond those acquired through practical command alone. Sun Quan urged Lü Meng to read about history and the management of affairs. Lü Meng answered that his official workload was heavy. The exchange, preserved in material quoted by Pei Songzhi's commentary on the Records of the Three Kingdoms, presents Sun Quan as encouraging study alongside existing responsibilities. Lü Meng eventually took up the recommendation. He remained an officer while learning; there is no account of a long interruption to pursue full-time schooling, and the record does not provide a complete calendar of his reading. Some time later, Lu Su engaged Lü Meng in a discussion and recognized a change in his knowledge. The episode is widely remembered because an established colleague reassessed someone whose earlier reputation had been shaped by military experience rather than scholarship. Lu Su's response followed a substantive encounter. It was not simply an award granted for attendance or an assertion that Lü Meng had changed. The text connects encouragement, actual learning and a later opportunity to demonstrate a broader understanding. The source survives through layered historical transmission. Popular classroom versions give the dialogue a polished form, and those words should not be presented as the precise speech of each participant. Nor can this incident establish that reading was responsible for every subsequent military achievement. It documents a narrower sequence: a working officer was advised to study, he accepted and pursued learning, and a fellow officer subsequently evaluated him differently. The development was recognized through conversation, while the officer continued to operate within the demands of public service.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Meng's fifth line highlights a learner's willingness to receive guidance. The historical account of Lü Meng offers a specific example. Sun Quan recommended reading, Lü Meng initially referred to his heavy duties, and later he made time to learn. Lu Su's changed opinion appeared only after a conversation revealed knowledge that had not previously been evident. For people who already have experience, admitting a knowledge gap can feel inconvenient. Yet the relevant question is whether the missing knowledge affects decisions that must be made now. Identify one recurring issue, find reliable materials and ask someone informed to challenge your understanding. Then return to the work and see whether your analysis becomes clearer. Learning while employed is not the same as merely collecting qualifications. The source does not say Lü Meng learned through this Small Image; the comparison is retrospective. The historical dialogue was preserved and edited in later writings, so it cannot support invented private feelings or a precise study timetable. What remains meaningful is the observable movement from advice to practice and from practice to a colleague's revised assessment.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

Small Image original: 利禦寇，上下順也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「以果斷方式破除蒙昧；不宜做侵害者，適宜抵禦侵害。」《象傳》解釋：上方與下方順。

Historical event | Short narrative

During the Ming dynasty, communities along China's southeastern coast faced raids and unstable local security. Military officers had to respond with forces that could operate effectively in the field, not merely gather men carrying weapons. Qi Jiguang became associated with efforts to train troops against coastal raiders. Recruitment was only the first part of the task. A soldier who could use a weapon individually might still be unable to act effectively in a formation, particularly when several kinds of equipment had to be used together. Qi recruited men from Yiwu and organized training around selection, discipline and coordination. Soldiers were assigned roles and taught to work as a unit, taking account of spacing, movement and the different purposes of their weapons. Practising before an encounter was essential: a shouted order in combat could not substitute for earlier familiarity with the same movements. His military writings emphasized repeatable instruction and regulations that officers and men could put into practice rather than leaving discipline at the level of a general demand for bravery. The trained forces participated in campaigns against coastal raiding. The account of their development proceeds from insecurity in coastal regions to recruitment, organization and repeated drill, followed by operational use of the assembled force. Training did not remove every military uncertainty. Supply, terrain, the conduct of opponents and changing local circumstances also affected campaigns. Nor should the entire military record be assigned to the virtues of a single formation or commander. Other officers and ordinary soldiers carried out much of the labor of daily preparation and field service. The episode shows how a force was made usable through a sequence of administrative and practical steps. The source supports the importance Qi placed on coordinated action, but it does not establish exact words from every training session or guarantee that all units always performed as intended. The subsequent defensive work depended on maintaining instructions, discipline and cooperation after recruitment had ended. A military organization had to keep functioning beyond the moment when its members first assembled.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Meng's final line refers to defending against raiders through coordination between those above and below. Qi Jiguang's recruitment and training of troops in Yiwu provide a historical comparison: men had to learn compatible tasks, practise together and understand orders before they could operate as a unit against coastal threats. The organizational lesson is not that every group needs military discipline. It is that an agreed purpose must be supported by roles that people can actually carry out. In an emergency-response team, for example, assigning a coordinator without training participants in communication and handover procedures leaves the plan incomplete. Clear responsibilities and repeated practice make cooperation more reliable, while feedback from the people doing the work helps improve the system. This remains a retrospective interpretation. Qi's accounts do not establish that he designed his training around this passage of the Small Image. The military context also matters: ancient language about repelling raiders should not be used to endorse aggression. The historical story concerns organized defense and the practical demands of training, with outcomes still influenced by circumstances beyond the formation itself.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.
