In 158 BCE, Emperor Wen of the Western Han visited military camps while the empire faced security concerns on its northern frontier. At camps he had inspected earlier, the imperial procession had been allowed relatively easy entry. His visit to the camp at Xiliu, commanded by Zhou Yafu, unfolded differently. Soldiers guarding the gates refused to open them merely because the emperor's carriage had arrived. They explained that the camp operated under military commands and that entry required the appropriate authorization. The emperor's attendants could not make their status a substitute for the camp's established procedure. Only after the relevant message had been conveyed and permission secured did the procession pass through the gate. The differences continued inside. Military rules prohibited rapid driving within the camp, and the imperial party slowed its carriages accordingly. Zhou Yafu then received the visitor according to military etiquette rather than treating the encounter as a routine court appearance. The emperor eventually departed and expressed approval of the discipline he had observed. The Records of the Grand Historian presents these actions as a connected series of scenes: the initial refusal at the gate, the request for authorization, the restriction on movement, the meeting with the commander, and the emperor's later assessment. They illustrate what a military command system looked like when it operated even in the presence of the monarch. The gate guards did not prevent entry permanently, and Zhou Yafu did not reject the emperor's authority. The entry was completed through the procedure the camp already used. The later praise is also important to its chronology: those serving at the gate did not know at the beginning how the emperor would judge the experience. As with other ancient narrative histories, the account was composed after the events and cannot establish that every conversation was preserved word for word. Nor can a single inspection show that Emperor Wen always respected regulations elsewhere. What this episode records is one visit in which orders were enforced, permission was obtained, and the commander received the emperor without suspending the camp's discipline. King Zhao of Chu fell ill late in the Spring and Autumn period. The illness was a concern to the ruler and his ministers, who considered religious explanations and possible ceremonies within the practices of their time. A divination was reported to connect the illness with a river deity. This prompted ministers to propose an offering to the Yellow River. The proposal placed a geographical question directly before the court: which waters and mountains fell within Chu's ritual responsibility, and which lay outside it? The ministers put the proposed ceremony before the king. King Zhao rejected it. According to the account preserved in the Zuozhuan under Duke Ai's sixth year, he did not regard the Yellow River as one of the waters for which Chu was responsible. An illness did not, in his response, justify extending state sacrifice beyond that established territorial scope. The proposed ritual was therefore not carried out as urged by the ministers. The contrast in the recorded exchange is between a response prompted by a diagnosis through divination and a response grounded in the customary limits of royal ritual. The surviving passage does not demonstrate that the diviners consulted a particular hexagram of the Zhouyi. The source does not document a modern clinical assessment, and there is no warrant for inventing additional treatments or conversation. King Zhao's response stands as a documented choice within ancient ritual governance, while the progress of his illness must not be rewritten as a test of supernatural prediction.

In 154 BCE the Rebellion of the Seven States challenged the Western Han government. Rebel forces from Wu and Chu advanced, placing Liang under pressure. The Han court appointed Zhou Yafu to command an army. Liang urgently wanted relief, while Zhou had to consider the enemy’s supplies and the position of his own troops. Zhou Yafu held his position and worked to interrupt the Wu–Chu forces’ supply route rather than seeking an immediate frontal decision on terms set by the rebels. Liang continued to suffer pressure, and the decision not to rush directly to its aid provoked political dissatisfaction. Meanwhile, the rebels faced increasingly difficult provisioning. When they withdrew, Zhou took the opportunity to strike. The eventual defeat of the rebels came after a sequence of holding, disrupting supply, and attacking. The outcome did not cancel the danger faced by Liang. This account distinguishes a commander’s observable deployment from any unrecorded private feelings, and it should not turn a disputed strategic decision into a universally applicable formula. Liang’s appeals occurred while rebel forces remained an immediate threat. Zhou’s method depended on maintaining Han positions for long enough that the interrupted rebel supply line mattered. He could not simply announce that the opponents would run short of provisions; the deployment had to remain in effect until their situation changed. The later attack followed a change in the field circumstances, not merely a calendar deadline. For Zhou Yafu, the pressure on Liang and the pressure on rebel provisions were connected but not identical problems. Protecting the broader campaign by targeting food supply could require patience even while an allied region requested immediate relief. Maintaining the Han position in the meantime was essential; leaving a supply route interrupted only briefly would not create the same conditions. The rebel withdrawal then offered a different military situation from the one at the start. This difference between the initial crisis and the later opportunity is necessary to understand his campaign.

After the Shu campaign entered Longyou, the position at Jieting became critical to the continuation of Zhuge Liang’s first northern expedition. Ma Su was entrusted with local command. His deployment failed to hold the position, and the campaign could no longer proceed on its original assumptions. The importance of Jieting lay in its connection to the rest of the expedition, not simply in its name on a map. With Jieting lost, Zhuge Liang withdrew his forces. A withdrawal required soldiers and their officers to abandon the planned advance and return to a more defensible arrangement; the decision did not erase the costs already incurred. Zhuge Liang then submitted a memorial requesting a reduction of his own rank. The memorial acknowledged his responsibility for the choice of commander rather than assigning the entire failure to a subordinate. The military loss, the withdrawal, and the memorial were separate stages of the same episode. The surviving record supports this sequence, but it does not justify importing the fictional Empty Fort Stratagem into it. The episode also cannot establish that one appointment alone explained every aspect of the campaign’s failure. The site mattered because an advancing army could not move independently of its supporting positions. Once the approach became untenable, the remaining forces needed a withdrawal instead of continuing along the original route. The memorial is relevant precisely because it appears after the failure, when the commander was reviewing responsibility for decisions already made. Neither the act of retreating nor the statement of responsibility reverses the loss of the position. The command structure also mattered after the immediate battlefield reversal. The responsibility for appointing Ma Su was not identical to the responsibility for every action taken at Jieting, yet it was a decision Zhuge Liang could acknowledge in a formal document. When troops were withdrawn, that act changed the options available for the remaining expedition. The army could no longer pursue the same regional goals by the original sequence. This is why a full account connects the military reversal to the subsequent official response rather than treating the loss and the memorial as unrelated anecdotes.

As Qin authority collapsed, rival armies advanced toward the Guanzhong region, where the former imperial capital and its surrounding communities faced a change of rulers. Liu Bang entered the area with armed followers. For residents who had experienced Qin administration and the disruption of war, the immediate questions were practical: which laws would remain, how soldiers would behave, and who could enforce the new promises. Military arrival alone could not settle those uncertainties. According to the historical account in the Records of the Grand Historian, Liu Bang assembled local elders and announced a simplified set of three legal provisions. The measure is conventionally remembered as the Three-Article Covenant. It addressed serious offenses while abandoning many burdens associated in the account with the former regime. The announcement was also a public undertaking by an advancing commander. Its credibility depended on the conduct of the occupying forces after the announcement, not merely on the wording of the proclamation. The immediate sequence was therefore the collapse of Qin control, the entry of Liu Bang's forces, a meeting with local representatives, and the presentation of rules that residents could understand. Soldiers still had to maintain order under those rules. Local families continued living amid political uncertainty, because other contenders had not disappeared. Xiang Yu remained a powerful military rival, and decisions about who would ultimately control Guanzhong were not concluded by the covenant. The declaration became an important element in later accounts of Liu Bang's ability to obtain local cooperation. Yet the larger struggle continued beyond this episode, eventually developing into competition among the forces that had helped destroy Qin rule. Neither the announcement nor its favorable portrayal in historical writing proves that all inhabitants approved, or that every subsequent action followed the same standard. The documented episode is a change of authority accompanied by a publicly stated legal commitment; what happened afterward depended on continued military and political developments.

Historical event | Short narrative

Between the Sui and Tang periods, the Chinese state gradually gave examinations a larger part in selecting some officials. Earlier appointment practices and family connections continued to matter, but subjects such as the jinshi examination opened an additional route through which educated men might seek public office. The change was gradual and was not implemented everywhere or for everyone in an identical form. Studying for an examination required books, instruction and time; travel to a place of assessment could impose further expense. As the examination route developed, candidates prepared written work and sought to meet requirements established by the government. Those who passed still faced the separate process of appointment, and not every successful candidate received an office immediately. The system also existed alongside other avenues to public service. It did not eliminate the importance of family wealth, social networks or access to education. For individuals without a powerful lineage the examinations could provide opportunities, yet differences in resources continued to shape who could realistically participate. Over subsequent generations the role and organization of civil examinations expanded and changed. Historians debate details of when particular subjects began and at what point the system acquired its later institutional form. Consequently, it would be inaccurate to assign the mature imperial examination system to a single founding day. The documented sequence instead moves from adjustments in recruitment, through the establishment and use of examination subjects, to further development under later dynasties. Passing a test was one stage in that process rather than automatic entry into government. The surviving history supports an account of changing pathways to office, not a fictional account of a particular candidate's private struggles or a claim that effort guaranteed promotion. This distinction is necessary when adapting institutional history into a short narrative. What can be described is the evolving institution rather than the thoughts or fortunes of an invented examination candidate. The difference matters for readers.

After the founding of the republic, Yuan Shikai occupied a commanding position in the central government, but his relationship with provincial and political interests remained complicated. In 1915 he moved to replace the republican form of government with a monarchy, changing the political framework under which existing offices had operated. Support for the imperial project was not universal. Opposition appeared in public politics and then in the National Protection War. Provincial leaders and forces that had previously cooperated with Yuan did not necessarily accept the new constitutional claim. Political disagreement thus had military as well as institutional consequences. In 1916 Yuan abandoned the monarchical project. That reversal did not remove the political conflicts surrounding the distribution of power. The surviving sequence is a proposed imperial restoration, widening opposition, war, and cancellation. It is not evidence that every supporter or opponent held the same motives. The attempt to create a monarchy altered the stated basis on which offices operated after the founding of the republic. That change required recognition from provinces, officers, and political groupings whose cooperation was not guaranteed. Opposition during the National Protection War made the weakness of that recognition visible. Cancellation of the project in 1916 was a direct response to a changed political situation, not an announcement that restored every previous relationship. The affair therefore traces a move from a proposed institutional transformation to resistance, fighting, withdrawal of the claim, and continuing instability. In the Sui dynasty, the court undertook construction of Renshou Palace outside the principal capital. Building materials had to be obtained and transported, craftspeople organized, and substantial labor mobilized. These requirements meant that the project affected people and resources well beyond the finished palace grounds. Work proceeded under officials responsible for carrying out the ruler's building program. The visible result could be assessed only after construction, whereas the burdens of procurement and labor began much earlier. The historical tradition describes the project as extravagant and connects its execution with controversy over the treatment of workers and the use of public resources. The opening of a palace did not cancel obligations incurred during construction. Historical event | Short narrative

During the Warring States period, Qin offered cities in exchange for the prized He Shi jade belonging to Zhao. The Zhao court feared that sending the object might result in its loss without the promised territory, while rejecting the request risked confrontation with a stronger state. Lin Xiangru was chosen to carry the jade to Qin and negotiate. At the Qin court, the exchange did not move directly toward the delivery of cities. Lin arranged to regain possession of the jade and used ceremonial procedures to preserve room for negotiation. He then made arrangements for the object to be returned to Zhao while he remained to face Qin’s ruler. The two sides did not complete the proposed exchange on the terms initially presented. The narrative in the Records of the Grand Historian includes developed speeches, which are ancient literary representations rather than verifiable stenographic transcripts. The central actions—dispatch, negotiation, return of the jade, and Lin’s continued presence—form the historical story. Qin and Zhao did not suddenly become equal powers because this particular negotiation ended without the loss of the jade. The jade was the physical object at the center of negotiations, but the promised cities were the political condition attached to its transfer. Returning the object separated possession from further bargaining. Lin’s continued presence in Qin after its removal meant that the immediate task and the safety of the envoy were no longer the same issue. Ancient reported speeches can illuminate the narrative structure without being repeated as authenticated words. Zhao’s original predicament involved two unequal risks, because losing the jade and provoking Qin were both possible. The court’s decision to send an envoy allowed negotiation rather than immediate refusal, but gave Lin a responsibility to safeguard the object. His actions at Qin changed the bargaining situation by recovering control of the jade. The separation of the jade’s return from his own departure is particularly important: it shows that the object was protected before the envoy was free of danger. The eventual outcome did not fulfill the proposed exchange of cities.

Neither Sun Quan nor Liu Bei entered the relationship without an existing political position to defend. Any joint response to Cao Cao required representatives to establish which aims genuinely overlapped. Military cooperation could follow only after enough terms were understood to allow joint operations. The success of the confrontation at Red Cliffs then changed the immediate balance, but it did not create a common administration of all lands claimed by the partners. The subsequent disagreements remind us that the chronology of an alliance extends beyond its best-known battle.

By the late nineteenth century, the Qing government and regional officials had already invested in modern naval vessels, weapons production, and technical education. In 1894, war between Qing China and Japan put the existing military system under the pressure of major operations on land and at sea. Forces that had developed through separate institutions now had to confront an opponent in a connected conflict. Naval vessels needed supplies and repairs, land forces depended on transport and reliable command, and information had to move among officials responsible for different parts of the war. The Qing armies and fleets suffered defeats during the campaign. The failure of particular operations exposed difficulties in organization and military cooperation that equipment purchases alone had not resolved. These results should not erase the technical work achieved before the war, but they do show that tools and institutions are not interchangeable. Military defeat was followed by diplomatic negotiations. In 1895 the Qing government signed the Treaty of Shimonoseki, under which Taiwan and the Penghu Islands were ceded to Japan. That agreement carried the consequences of the fighting beyond the battlefield and changed the political circumstances of people living in the territories transferred. The sequence ran from earlier acquisition of modern weapons and infrastructure, through wartime performance, to a settlement imposing territorial and financial obligations. Historical event | Short narrative

In 1906 the Qing court announced preparations for constitutional government amid increasing demands for political change. Reform advocates expected a meaningful alteration in the exercise of power, while the imperial court retained an interest in preserving ultimate authority. The proposed transition involved not only constitutional language but also dates, representative bodies and the question of what influence those bodies would actually possess. The court published staged preparations and established provincial consultative assemblies and a national advisory institution. These organizations created new arenas for political activity, but supporters of constitutionalism continued to assess whether the process matched its promises. Questions about timing and the powers reserved to the throne remained divisive. The composition of the cabinet established in 1911 intensified criticism that meaningful authority had not been redistributed as anticipated. Confidence in the program weakened while revolutionary and regional political developments gathered pace. The dynasty fell in a broader crisis that cannot be explained by one appointment alone. The sequence includes the original promise, a series of institutional steps, disputes about their substance, and a decline in trust before the end of imperial rule. The historical sequence depends on several different kinds of action: an initial political or military problem, a response by people in positions to act, and an aftermath in which the arrangements still had to be implemented. Where a source summarizes a long period, it does not provide a day-by-day account or justify assigning motives to every participant. A decision recorded in a history is not necessarily the same as the practical result it was intended to produce. Orders, discussions and appointments are identifiable moments; their implementation affects officials, troops or residents afterward. Maintaining that distinction is necessary to preserve the chronology without treating a later outcome as inevitable. The surviving sources allow the episode to be told in this order without recreating conversations or inner thoughts. They do not establish that everyone affected welcomed the decision, nor do they allow a single person or one written announcement to stand for all the later events.

In 1449, the Ming emperor Yingzong accompanied a military expedition northward against the Oirat forces. The presence of the ruler made the campaign more than a frontier operation: the movement of the army also exposed the central court to the fortunes of an expedition far from Beijing. A large military column depended on supplies, transport, reliable orders and coordination during its advance and return. The Ming forces encountered serious difficulties on the march. During the withdrawal, the army suffered a crushing defeat in the area known as Tumu, and the emperor was captured. The scale of the reverse cannot be explained by a single decision or an unverified figure for the numbers involved. Command, logistics, routes and the opposing army's actions all formed part of the conditions under which the disaster occurred. News of the defeat reached Beijing while the emperor was still in captivity. Civil and military officials then faced a linked set of urgent tasks. They had to arrange the city's defense, organize command and consider how government would operate without the sovereign present. The military defeat thus moved quickly from an expedition's route into the institutions of the capital. The measures taken in Beijing were a response to the crisis, not a sign that its outcome had been foreseen at the expedition's outset. The essential chronology is the decision to conduct the campaign, the emperor's participation, difficulties on the return, the defeat at Tumu, his capture, and the reorganization of defense and government at the capital. Historical accounts differ in their evaluation of individuals and in some numerical details. Those uncertainties should not be filled with invented scenes or reported speech. The event demonstrates that the consequences of military failure could extend beyond the battlefield, affecting political authority and daily administration while the immediate struggle remained unresolved.

Historical event | Short narrative

The 1911 Revolution created a need for government institutions capable of representing the republican movement and conducting ordinary administration. Several provinces had broken with the Qing court, but their declarations did not automatically establish a unified national budget, bureaucracy, or chain of military command. On 1 January 1912, Sun Yat-sen took office as provisional president in Nanjing. The provisional government organized offices and issued documents intended to translate political change into administration. Officials began operating under new institutional names while negotiations with the Qing side and other powers continued. The provisional government’s direct control remained geographically and financially limited. Appointing officers, communicating instructions, and sustaining institutions required support beyond the ceremony of inauguration. The case therefore extends from revolutionary declarations through institutional formation into continuing struggles over practical authority. The new government needed departments capable of exchanging documents, receiving information, and carrying out orders. The fact that provinces endorsed a republican direction did not mean they had surrendered their tax income or control of troops to one office. The provisional government’s early actions must therefore be understood alongside the limits of its resources and the continuing negotiations with northern authorities. The installation of a provisional president provided a recognizable formal start to government in Nanjing, but it did not mean every part of the country was administered from that office. Ministries and civil officers needed resources and procedures to turn documents into action. Provinces that had separated from Qing rule still exercised influence over their own forces and revenues. Negotiation with northern leaders continued while the new government undertook daily business. That overlap between institutional founding and contested authority is central to the chronology and explains why inauguration alone could not complete the revolution’s work. Every institution still had to secure cooperation and resources in order to operate beyond its founding announcements.

Historical event | Short narrative

Early in the Tang dynasty, the court faced tension between Crown Prince Li Jiancheng and Li Shimin, who had military achievements and supporters of his own. The succession arrangement gave Li Jiancheng the position of heir, but powerful factions competed over the distribution of political and military authority. In 626, Li Shimin used armed force at Xuanwu Gate. Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji were killed, and the existing route of succession was broken. Li Shimin secured the advantage at court and subsequently became emperor. The immediate outcome was a violent transfer of power, not an ordinary administrative succession. Later assessments of Emperor Taizong’s government concern what happened after the coup and cannot retroactively remove the deaths caused by it. Sources compiled under later political arrangements also require awareness of their perspectives. The incident illustrates a sequence of political rivalry, armed intervention, and a changed dynastic succession. The prince already had an established claim as the designated heir, while his rival possessed military and political resources. Violence at Xuanwu Gate changed which claim could be pursued. The deaths were immediate and irreversible, while the establishment of a new reign required subsequent court arrangements. Assessing the period therefore requires keeping the coup and the later record of government separate. The conflict cannot be described as simply replacing one holder of office with another. The position of crown prince had already been formally assigned, and competing support networks made succession a struggle over who would control the court and armed forces. Choosing force at a palace gate meant that the decision operated through killing rather than through the ordinary workings of succession. After the deaths, control had to be consolidated. After the Shu campaign entered Longyou, the position at Jieting became critical to the continuation of Zhuge Liang’s first northern expedition. Ma Su was entrusted with local command. His deployment failed to hold the position, and the campaign could no longer proceed on its original assumptions. The importance of Jieting lay in its connection to the rest of the expedition, not simply in its name on a map. With Jieting lost, Zhuge Liang withdrew his forces. A withdrawal required soldiers and their officers to abandon the planned advance and return to a more defensible arrangement; the decision did not erase the costs already incurred. Zhuge Liang then submitted a memorial requesting a reduction of his own rank. The memorial acknowledged his responsibility for the choice of commander rather than assigning the entire failure to a subordinate. The episode also cannot establish that one appointment alone explained every aspect of the campaign’s failure. Neither the act of retreating nor the statement of responsibility reverses the loss of the position. The command structure also mattered after the immediate battlefield reversal. When troops were withdrawn, that act changed the options available for the remaining expedition. The army could no longer pursue the same regional goals by the original sequence. Coastal communities in Ming China faced repeated attacks associated with the maritime raiders often called wokou. Local military defense required more than individual fighters, because men recruited from different places needed to understand common commands and how their weapons would be used together. Qi Jiguang sought recruits at Yiwu and placed particular importance on discipline and cooperation. The recruits were organized into units and trained in coordinated movement and the complementary use of weapons. Exercises gave officers a way to establish common procedures before combat. These arrangements were employed in campaigns against the raiders, while Qi also described training methods in his military writings. The process moved from recruitment to formation, repeated instruction and operations, rather than resting on a single ingenious battlefield maneuver. Results depended on terrain, provisioning, opponents and conditions beyond training alone. The available narrative can describe Qi’s recruitment and organization without inventing personal conversations among soldiers or claiming that every success followed from one formation. The lasting element is the effort to turn the capabilities of individuals into practical coordination under a shared command. The Han court’s competition with the Xiongnu led it to seek relationships with peoples in the Western Regions. Zhang Qian undertook a further mission, carrying Han proposals to Wusun and other groups. Traveling to those regions made communication possible, but it did not place local rulers under Han command. Zhang conveyed the court’s interest in cooperation. Wusun leaders had political arrangements and security concerns of their own, and their decisions could not be dictated by the arrival of a foreign envoy. The mission added to exchanges of people and information, while any lasting diplomatic connection required further contacts and decisions by multiple participants. Subsequent diplomatic visits and marriage arrangements belonged to later stages involving other people. It would therefore be misleading to attribute every later outcome to an agreement supposedly completed during Zhang’s visit. The mission covered long distances and dealt with political communities whose response depended on local circumstances. Information brought back from such journeys could inform future exchanges, but a proposal carried by an envoy was not itself a lasting alliance. Decisions on the Han side and decisions in Wusun formed distinct stages. The later pattern of diplomacy extended beyond the duration of Zhang’s personal mission. A messenger could carry the Han court’s intention but could not commit the Wusun government in its place. That distinction mattered because the same regional security situation looked different from the two political centers. The long journey also meant that information was exchanged in stages and later contacts might be needed to clarify proposals. Zhang’s mission formed part of a growing network of contact, and subsequent diplomatic developments took place over time. The account should not assign later marriage negotiations or alliances to an agreement for which this specific mission supplies no proof.

Historical event | Short narrative

In 154 BCE the Rebellion of the Seven States challenged the Western Han government. Rebel forces from Wu and Chu advanced, placing Liang under pressure. The Han court appointed Zhou Yafu to command an army. Liang urgently wanted relief, while Zhou had to consider the enemy’s supplies and the position of his own troops. Zhou Yafu held his position and worked to interrupt the Wu–Chu forces’ supply route rather than seeking an immediate frontal decision on terms set by the rebels. Liang continued to suffer pressure, and the decision not to rush directly to its aid provoked political dissatisfaction. Meanwhile, the rebels faced increasingly difficult provisioning. When they withdrew, Zhou took the opportunity to strike. The eventual defeat of the rebels came after a sequence of holding, disrupting supply, and attacking. The outcome did not cancel the danger faced by Liang. This account distinguishes a commander’s observable deployment from any unrecorded private feelings, and it should not turn a disputed strategic decision into a universally applicable formula. Liang’s appeals occurred while rebel forces remained an immediate threat. Zhou’s method depended on maintaining Han positions for long enough that the interrupted rebel supply line mattered. He could not simply announce that the opponents would run short of provisions; the deployment had to remain in effect until their situation changed. The later attack followed a change in the field circumstances, not merely a calendar deadline. For Zhou Yafu, the pressure on Liang and the pressure on rebel provisions were connected but not identical problems. Protecting the broader campaign by targeting food supply could require patience even while an allied region requested immediate relief. Maintaining the Han position in the meantime was essential; leaving a supply route interrupted only briefly would not create the same conditions. The rebel withdrawal then offered a different military situation from the one at the start. This difference between the initial crisis and the later opportunity is necessary to understand his campaign.

Historical event | Short narrative

Japan’s defeat in 1945 ended a major international war, but government and Communist forces in China still faced questions about the future political system, the distribution of territory and the command of armies. The National Government and representatives of the Chinese Communist Party did not hold identical positions on these matters. Avoiding another major war required not only statements of general principle but also decisions about forces and the administration of areas already under their control. Representatives met in Chongqing and produced the Summary of Conversations between Government and Communist Representatives, commonly called the Double Tenth Agreement. It recorded understandings about peace and national reconstruction. The document was an important public product of negotiation, yet several issues concerning armies and local authority remained unresolved. Military and political circumstances outside the meeting room continued to develop as the written understanding was announced. The agreement did not automatically settle the underlying power struggle or ensure that each party would implement every stated intention. Further conflict and unsuccessful efforts at cooperation followed. The event must therefore be told in three stages: the need for talks after the war, the publication of the agreement, and the continued difficulty of translating words into arrangements on the ground. The historical sequence depends on several different kinds of action: an initial political or military problem, a response by people in positions to act, and an aftermath in which the arrangements still had to be implemented. Historical event | Short narrative

In 1906 the Qing court announced preparations for constitutional government amid increasing demands for political change. Reform advocates expected a meaningful alteration in the exercise of power, while the imperial court retained an interest in preserving ultimate authority. The proposed transition involved not only constitutional language but also dates, representative bodies and the question of what influence those bodies would actually possess. The court published staged preparations and established provincial consultative assemblies and a national advisory institution. These organizations created new arenas for political activity, but supporters of constitutionalism continued to assess whether the process matched its promises. Questions about timing and the powers reserved to the throne remained divisive. The composition of the cabinet established in 1911 intensified criticism that meaningful authority had not been redistributed as anticipated. Confidence in the program weakened while revolutionary and regional political developments gathered pace. The dynasty fell in a broader crisis that cannot be explained by one appointment alone. The sequence includes the original promise, a series of institutional steps, disputes about their substance, and a decline in trust before the end of imperial rule. In 154 BCE the Rebellion of the Seven States challenged the Western Han government. Rebel forces from Wu and Chu advanced, placing Liang under pressure. Zhou Yafu held his position and worked to interrupt the Wu–Chu forces’ supply route rather than seeking an immediate frontal decision on terms set by the rebels. Liang continued to suffer pressure, and the decision not to rush directly to its aid provoked political dissatisfaction. Meanwhile, the rebels faced increasingly difficult provisioning. When they withdrew, Zhou took the opportunity to strike. The eventual defeat of the rebels came after a sequence of holding, disrupting supply, and attacking. Protecting the broader campaign by targeting food supply could require patience even while an allied region requested immediate relief. Maintaining the Han position in the meantime was essential; leaving a supply route interrupted only briefly would not create the same conditions. The rebel withdrawal then offered a different military situation from the one at the start. This difference between the initial crisis and the later opportunity is necessary to understand his campaign.

In 1449, the Ming emperor Yingzong accompanied a military expedition northward against the Oirat forces. The presence of the ruler made the campaign more than a frontier operation: the movement of the army also exposed the central court to the fortunes of an expedition far from Beijing. A large military column depended on supplies, transport, reliable orders and coordination during its advance and return. The Ming forces encountered serious difficulties on the march. During the withdrawal, the army suffered a crushing defeat in the area known as Tumu, and the emperor was captured. The scale of the reverse cannot be explained by a single decision or an unverified figure for the numbers involved. Command, logistics, routes and the opposing army's actions all formed part of the conditions under which the disaster occurred. News of the defeat reached Beijing while the emperor was still in captivity. Civil and military officials then faced a linked set of urgent tasks. They had to arrange the city's defense, organize command and consider how government would operate without the sovereign present. The military defeat thus moved quickly from an expedition's route into the institutions of the capital. The measures taken in Beijing were a response to the crisis, not a sign that its outcome had been foreseen at the expedition's outset. The essential chronology is the decision to conduct the campaign, the emperor's participation, difficulties on the return, the defeat at Tumu, his capture, and the reorganization of defense and government at the capital. Historical accounts differ in their evaluation of individuals and in some numerical details. Those uncertainties should not be filled with invented scenes or reported speech. The event demonstrates that the consequences of military failure could extend beyond the battlefield, affecting political authority and daily administration while the immediate struggle remained unresolved.

As Cao Cao's armies moved south into Jing Province, Liu Bei could no longer remain in his existing position. The crisis became acute at Changban. Pursuing forces struck Liu Bei's column, and the retreat turned into a serious defeat and dispersal. People accompanying the army faced danger as the military position collapsed. The surviving troops and leaders could not treat the withdrawal as a completed plan; they had to find one another and identify where enough men could gather to continue. Contact with Sun Quan then offered a possible route to cooperation against Cao Cao. The subsequent alliance did not erase the losses at Changban or mean that the retreat had been designed from the beginning as a route to a successful coalition. The historical sequence therefore runs from the loss of a position in Jing, through a hazardous withdrawal and defeat at Changban, to the gradual reassembly of surviving forces and attempts to find external support. The movement was shaped by a pursuing army and by the needs of people following Liu Bei. Its aftermath included both a retained political-military presence and the human cost of the retreat. It should not be rewritten as an effortless strategic escape.

After the Shu campaign entered Longyou, the position at Jieting became critical to the continuation of Zhuge Liang’s first northern expedition. Ma Su was entrusted with local command. His deployment failed to hold the position, and the campaign could no longer proceed on its original assumptions. The importance of Jieting lay in its connection to the rest of the expedition, not simply in its name on a map. With Jieting lost, Zhuge Liang withdrew his forces. A withdrawal required soldiers and their officers to abandon the planned advance and return to a more defensible arrangement; the decision did not erase the costs already incurred. Zhuge Liang then submitted a memorial requesting a reduction of his own rank. The memorial acknowledged his responsibility for the choice of commander rather than assigning the entire failure to a subordinate. The military loss, the withdrawal, and the memorial were separate stages of the same episode. The surviving record supports this sequence, but it does not justify importing the fictional Empty Fort Stratagem into it. The episode also cannot establish that one appointment alone explained every aspect of the campaign’s failure. The site mattered because an advancing army could not move independently of its supporting positions. Once the approach became untenable, the remaining forces needed a withdrawal instead of continuing along the original route. The memorial is relevant precisely because it appears after the failure, when the commander was reviewing responsibility for decisions already made. In the early years of the Three Kingdoms era, Lü Meng was already serving Sun Quan as a military officer in the lower Yangtze region. His duties involved troops and campaigns, yet these responsibilities did not eliminate the need to understand earlier wars, institutions, and political decisions. Sun Quan urged him to undertake regular reading. According to an account quoted by Pei Songzhi in his commentary on the Records of the Three Kingdoms, the ruler did not expect Lü Meng to abandon military service and become a professional classical scholar. He wanted an officer with practical responsibilities to gain broader historical knowledge. Lü Meng first pointed to his demanding schedule. Sun Quan replied by referring to the burdens of his own position and argued that work need not make study impossible. The surviving narrative conveys the substance of that exchange; the polished dialogue familiar from later teaching materials should not be mistaken for a verbatim record. Lü Meng accepted the advice and began to read while continuing his existing duties. He was not reassigned from his post simply to become a student, and the change was not completed in a single meeting. Learning had to fit around work already under way. The later part of the account introduces Lu Su, another important officer. When the two discussed affairs, Lu Su recognized that Lü Meng had acquired knowledge and judgment beyond his earlier reputation. The resulting reassessment by a colleague marks the recorded outcome of the educational episode. It does not establish that every subsequent campaign succeeded because of reading or that any particular text supplied a military plan. The sequence in the surviving source is nevertheless clear: Sun Quan noticed a gap between experience and knowledge, recommended study, Lü Meng followed that recommendation while remaining at work, and Lu Su later acknowledged a change in his ability to discuss public affairs. The account describes a professional development process, not a miraculous transformation or evidence that anyone used the Small Image commentary to direct it.

Historical event | Short narrative

Between the Sui and Tang periods, the Chinese state gradually gave examinations a larger part in selecting some officials. Earlier appointment practices and family connections continued to matter, but subjects such as the jinshi examination opened an additional route through which educated men might seek public office. The change was gradual and was not implemented everywhere or for everyone in an identical form. Studying for an examination required books, instruction and time; travel to a place of assessment could impose further expense. As the examination route developed, candidates prepared written work and sought to meet requirements established by the government. Those who passed still faced the separate process of appointment, and not every successful candidate received an office immediately. The system also existed alongside other avenues to public service. It did not eliminate the importance of family wealth, social networks or access to education. For individuals without a powerful lineage the examinations could provide opportunities, yet differences in resources continued to shape who could realistically participate. Over subsequent generations the role and organization of civil examinations expanded and changed. Historians debate details of when particular subjects began and at what point the system acquired its later institutional form. Consequently, it would be inaccurate to assign the mature imperial examination system to a single founding day. The documented sequence instead moves from adjustments in recruitment, through the establishment and use of examination subjects, to further development under later dynasties. Passing a test was one stage in that process rather than automatic entry into government. The surviving history supports an account of changing pathways to office, not a fictional account of a particular candidate's private struggles or a claim that effort guaranteed promotion. This distinction is necessary when adapting institutional history into a short narrative. What can be described is the evolving institution rather than the thoughts or fortunes of an invented examination candidate. The difference matters for readers.

In 1949, plans for a new central government unfolded while the military and administrative control of different parts of China was changing. Groups participating in the political consultation process had to decide how they would describe the new state and distribute responsibilities among its institutions. A common written framework could give the new organizations a declared set of arrangements, but it could not by itself establish day-to-day administration in every locality. The first plenary session of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference adopted the Common Program and dealt with the organization of central authorities. Participants agreed to a framework for the new government and its policy orientation. The document supplied terms under which offices, officials and departments could subsequently work. Its adoption was a distinct political step taken by the assembled participants, not an act of direct voting by the entire population. Following the meeting, institutions still had to appoint personnel, issue rules and carry out administration. Political and military authority was not identical everywhere at the moment of adoption. The conference thus produced an identifiable institutional foundation, but the subsequent work of implementing that foundation remained dependent on actual administration, political support and territorial conditions. The historical sequence depends on several different kinds of action: an initial political or military problem, a response by people in positions to act, and an aftermath in which the arrangements still had to be implemented. Historical event | Short narrative

After the founding of the republic, Yuan Shikai occupied a commanding position in the central government, but his relationship with provincial and political interests remained complicated. In 1915 he moved to replace the republican form of government with a monarchy, changing the political framework under which existing offices had operated. Support for the imperial project was not universal. Opposition appeared in public politics and then in the National Protection War. Provincial leaders and forces that had previously cooperated with Yuan did not necessarily accept the new constitutional claim. Political disagreement thus had military as well as institutional consequences. In 1916 Yuan abandoned the monarchical project. That reversal did not remove the political conflicts surrounding the distribution of power. The surviving sequence is a proposed imperial restoration, widening opposition, war, and cancellation. It is not evidence that every supporter or opponent held the same motives. The change in regime title required not just central announcement but acceptance by officials and armed forces across the country. Provinces responded under circumstances that did not always match the central government’s expectations. As armed opposition expanded, the effectiveness of proclamations depended on military control and local cooperation. Ending the imperial claim was an identifiable reversal, but not the end of the political crisis. The attempt to create a monarchy altered the stated basis on which offices operated after the founding of the republic. That change required recognition from provinces, officers, and political groupings whose cooperation was not guaranteed. Opposition during the National Protection War made the weakness of that recognition visible. Cancellation of the project in 1916 was a direct response to a changed political situation, not an announcement that restored every previous relationship. The affair therefore traces a move from a proposed institutional transformation to resistance, fighting, withdrawal of the claim, and continuing instability.

English editorial reading focus: Leaving danger may itself exact a price (thematic heading, not a literal translation of the original).

Historical event | Short narrative

A succession conflict in the state of Jin forced Chong'er to leave the political position he had once occupied. With companions who remained alongside him, he spent years moving among other states. As an exile, he did not command the administrative and military resources of Jin. His situation depended on whether other rulers received him, offered provisions or chose to become involved in Jin's affairs. The treatment he received was not uniform. Some hosts offered assistance, while other encounters brought less favorable treatment. Throughout these travels, Chong'er and his followers had to maintain their association without a secure timetable for returning home. The record presents a succession of contacts and shifting circumstances, rather than a single, uninterrupted plan that carried him straight to the throne. There is no sound basis for assigning private thoughts to every host or for creating conversations missing from the surviving accounts. Eventually the state of Qin provided support that helped Chong'er return to Jin. He became ruler, later known as Duke Wen of Jin. His accession followed both the long period abroad and changes within Jin that made a return possible. Assistance from Qin mattered, but external backing alone would not explain every development within the state he was returning to. The order is important. First came the succession struggle and departure; then many years of movement, dependency and changing receptions; finally a political opening and Qin's assistance enabled a return and accession. His subsequent rule belongs to the aftermath, not to a destiny established on the day of his exile. Looking back from the eventual result can obscure how uncertain his position was during those years. The history supports a story of political displacement, enduring relationships and a later restoration, not a guarantee that every exile who waits will gain power. The aftermath must be distinguished from the original decision and evaluated from the surviving record.

As Cao Cao's armies moved south into Jing Province, Liu Bei could no longer remain in his existing position. The route south placed these different groups under pressure as Cao Cao's pursuit approached. There was no guarantee that everyone who had set out together could stay together during the movement. The crisis became acute at Changban. Pursuing forces struck Liu Bei's column, and the retreat turned into a serious defeat and dispersal. People accompanying the army faced danger as the military position collapsed. The surviving troops and leaders could not treat the withdrawal as a completed plan; they had to find one another and identify where enough men could gather to continue. The record does not allow the experience of each civilian or soldier to be reconstructed, nor does it support inventing a single conversation that determined the outcome. Contact with Sun Quan then offered a possible route to cooperation against Cao Cao. The subsequent alliance did not erase the losses at Changban or mean that the retreat had been designed from the beginning as a route to a successful coalition. The historical sequence therefore runs from the loss of a position in Jing, through a hazardous withdrawal and defeat at Changban, to the gradual reassembly of surviving forces and attempts to find external support. The movement was shaped by a pursuing army and by the needs of people following Liu Bei. Its aftermath included both a retained political-military presence and the human cost of the retreat. It should not be rewritten as an effortless strategic escape.

In 1911 the Wuchang uprising triggered a widening challenge to Qing authority. Provinces successively announced separation from the Qing government, although the participants did not all agree on the future political settlement. Military conflict and negotiations between northern and southern leaders proceeded in parallel. In 1912 the Qing emperor abdicated and a republican political form replaced the dynasty’s monarchy. The abdication represented a specific institutional break, but it followed multiple provincial decisions, military actions, and political exchanges. The change cannot be assigned exclusively to one individual or one day of armed uprising. After the abdication, military forces, officials, and local governments still had to determine how they related to the new central institutions. The establishment of a republic did not resolve every question of finance and authority. The historical outcome involved the end of an old regime and the beginning of another period of negotiation. A province declaring separation from the Qing did not by itself determine the legal position of other provinces or the national government. Military advances and conversations over an acceptable settlement occurred side by side. After the emperor’s abdication, offices and armed organizations still required new chains of responsibility. That practical aftermath was part of the revolution’s political transformation. The revolutionary sequence included armed resistance and negotiated institutional settlement. Provincial defections weakened the Qing administration, while those negotiating in the north and south still faced the issue of how military forces would fit into a new order. The emperor’s abdication ended the dynasty’s formal monarchy; it did not instantly give every locality an agreed set of administrative procedures. The subsequent question was how officials, armies, and budgets would operate under republican institutions. This is why the story continues beyond the best-known date of the imperial abdication. The formal constitutional change and the practical transfer of authority did not happen simultaneously across the whole territory.

The episode has a clear progression: competition following Qin's fall prompted the meeting; Liu Bang entered a stronger rival's camp; intermediaries managed communication and departure; and he returned from the encounter while the broader struggle continued. Under Emperor Xuanzong, Tang China enjoyed a period of prosperity and territorial reach. At the same time, frontier commanders accumulated troops and regional resources. Relations between the central government and frontier military authorities created tensions that could not be measured simply by prosperity at court. In 755 An Lushan launched his revolt. The rebellion placed severe military pressure on the Tang government, and Xuanzong eventually left Chang’an. Years of fighting disrupted population patterns, government revenue, and the political balance between the court and regional authorities. The outbreak in 755 was a recognizable turning point within developments that had accumulated over time. The effects continued long after the initial rising. Regional military and fiscal arrangements changed amid the struggle. The history should not be reduced to dramatic tales of palace life or presented as the result of a single character flaw. The roles of commanders, institutions, war, and local populations form the wider account. The Tang court’s earlier material success coexisted with a distribution of military resources that made frontier commanders unusually powerful. Once armed rebellion began, districts faced problems of military occupation, moving populations, and disrupted collection of revenue. These consequences developed beyond the initial year of revolt. The beginning of the war is easier to date than the completion of all its institutional effects. The political arrangement that allowed powerful frontier commanders to maintain local military resources already existed during the period described as prosperous. Those arrangements became especially significant when An Lushan rose against the court. As the conflict spread, the government had to manage competing demands of military defense, a displaced population, and weakened revenue. The effect on regional authority lasted beyond the date of the rebellion’s outbreak. A story limited to the rebellion’s initial announcement would omit precisely the longer consequences that made it a turning point in Tang political history.

Historical event | Short narrative

The 1911 Revolution created a need for government institutions capable of representing the republican movement and conducting ordinary administration. Several provinces had broken with the Qing court, but their declarations did not automatically establish a unified national budget, bureaucracy, or chain of military command. On 1 January 1912, Sun Yat-sen took office as provisional president in Nanjing. The provisional government organized offices and issued documents intended to translate political change into administration. Officials began operating under new institutional names while negotiations with the Qing side and other powers continued. The provisional government’s direct control remained geographically and financially limited. Appointing officers, communicating instructions, and sustaining institutions required support beyond the ceremony of inauguration. The case therefore extends from revolutionary declarations through institutional formation into continuing struggles over practical authority. The new government needed departments capable of exchanging documents, receiving information, and carrying out orders. The fact that provinces endorsed a republican direction did not mean they had surrendered their tax income or control of troops to one office. The provisional government’s early actions must therefore be understood alongside the limits of its resources and the continuing negotiations with northern authorities. The installation of a provisional president provided a recognizable formal start to government in Nanjing, but it did not mean every part of the country was administered from that office. Ministries and civil officers needed resources and procedures to turn documents into action. Provinces that had separated from Qing rule still exercised influence over their own forces and revenues. Negotiation with northern leaders continued while the new government undertook daily business. That overlap between institutional founding and contested authority is central to the chronology and explains why inauguration alone could not complete the revolution’s work. Every institution still had to secure cooperation and resources in order to operate beyond its founding announcements.

Historical event | Short narrative

In 158 BCE, Emperor Wen of the Western Han visited military camps while the empire faced security concerns on its northern frontier. At camps he had inspected earlier, the imperial procession had been allowed relatively easy entry. His visit to the camp at Xiliu, commanded by Zhou Yafu, unfolded differently. Soldiers guarding the gates refused to open them merely because the emperor's carriage had arrived. They explained that the camp operated under military commands and that entry required the appropriate authorization. The emperor's attendants could not make their status a substitute for the camp's established procedure. Only after the relevant message had been conveyed and permission secured did the procession pass through the gate. The differences continued inside. Military rules prohibited rapid driving within the camp, and the imperial party slowed its carriages accordingly. Zhou Yafu then received the visitor according to military etiquette rather than treating the encounter as a routine court appearance. The emperor eventually departed and expressed approval of the discipline he had observed. The Records of the Grand Historian presents these actions as a connected series of scenes: the initial refusal at the gate, the request for authorization, the restriction on movement, the meeting with the commander, and the emperor's later assessment. They illustrate what a military command system looked like when it operated even in the presence of the monarch. The gate guards did not prevent entry permanently, and Zhou Yafu did not reject the emperor's authority. The entry was completed through the procedure the camp already used. The later praise is also important to its chronology: those serving at the gate did not know at the beginning how the emperor would judge the experience. As with other ancient narrative histories, the account was composed after the events and cannot establish that every conversation was preserved word for word. Nor can a single inspection show that Emperor Wen always respected regulations elsewhere. What this episode records is one visit in which orders were enforced, permission was obtained, and the commander received the emperor without suspending the camp's discipline. In 154 BCE the Rebellion of the Seven States challenged the Western Han government. Rebel forces from Wu and Chu advanced, placing Liang under pressure. Zhou Yafu held his position and worked to interrupt the Wu–Chu forces’ supply route rather than seeking an immediate frontal decision on terms set by the rebels. Liang continued to suffer pressure, and the decision not to rush directly to its aid provoked political dissatisfaction. Meanwhile, the rebels faced increasingly difficult provisioning. When they withdrew, Zhou took the opportunity to strike. The eventual defeat of the rebels came after a sequence of holding, disrupting supply, and attacking. The outcome did not cancel the danger faced by Liang. This account distinguishes a commander’s observable deployment from any unrecorded private feelings, and it should not turn a disputed strategic decision into a universally applicable formula. Liang’s appeals occurred while rebel forces remained an immediate threat. Zhou’s method depended on maintaining Han positions for long enough that the interrupted rebel supply line mattered. He could not simply announce that the opponents would run short of provisions; the deployment had to remain in effect until their situation changed. The later attack followed a change in the field circumstances, not merely a calendar deadline. For Zhou Yafu, the pressure on Liang and the pressure on rebel provisions were connected but not identical problems. Protecting the broader campaign by targeting food supply could require patience even while an allied region requested immediate relief. Maintaining the Han position in the meantime was essential; leaving a supply route interrupted only briefly would not create the same conditions. The rebel withdrawal then offered a different military situation from the one at the start. This difference between the initial crisis and the later opportunity is necessary to understand his campaign.

The arrangement addressed the immediate military confrontation, although it imposed continuing financial obligations. The affair therefore traces a move from a proposed institutional transformation to resistance, fighting, withdrawal of the claim, and continuing instability.

The recruits were organized into units and trained in coordinated movement and the complementary use of weapons. Exercises gave officers a way to establish common procedures before combat. These arrangements were employed in campaigns against the raiders, while Qi also described training methods in his military writings. The process moved from recruitment to formation, repeated instruction and operations, rather than resting on a single ingenious battlefield maneuver. Results depended on terrain, provisioning, opponents and conditions beyond training alone. The available narrative can describe Qi’s recruitment and organization without inventing personal conversations among soldiers or claiming that every success followed from one formation. The lasting element is the effort to turn the capabilities of individuals into practical coordination under a shared command. The historical sequence depends on several different kinds of action: an initial political or military problem, a response by people in positions to act, and an aftermath in which the arrangements still had to be implemented. Where a source summarizes a long period, it does not provide a day-by-day account or justify assigning motives to every participant. A decision recorded in a history is not necessarily the same as the practical result it was intended to produce. Orders, discussions and appointments are identifiable moments; their implementation affects officials, troops or residents afterward. Maintaining that distinction is necessary to preserve the chronology without treating a later outcome as inevitable. The surviving sources allow the episode to be told in this order without recreating conversations or inner thoughts. They do not establish that everyone affected welcomed the decision, nor do they allow a single person or one written announcement to stand for all the later events.

Small Image original: 已事遄往，尚合志也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「辦完自己的事便迅速前往援助，無咎；斟酌自己應減損多少。」《象傳》解釋：尚合志。

English editorial reading focus: Supporting a shared need without losing the resources required to act (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

During the struggle between Liu Bang and Xiang Yu, field armies repeatedly needed soldiers, food, and other supplies. Liu Bang’s access to the Guanzhong region provided an administrative and agricultural base, but that base would have contributed little if its civil government had ceased functioning. Frontline demands changed as campaigns continued. Xiao He remained primarily in Guanzhong and maintained administrative work. Population records, provisions, and the recruitment or replenishment of manpower formed part of the support reaching Liu Bang’s forces. These were not isolated tasks completed once at the beginning of the war. After troops consumed supplies and suffered losses, the rear organization had to replenish what could be provided and arrange onward transport. Historical accounts of the Chu–Han conflict mention Xiao He’s contribution alongside battlefield leadership. His administrative work helps explain how an army remained active across repeated engagements, but it does not erase the labor of local communities or prove that every request could be fulfilled. The story is about sustained support in the background of changing military events. The work depended on the continuing relationship between local administration and military operations. Registers mattered when manpower had to be identified; stored provisions mattered when supplies had to be prepared and moved. These connected activities took place before and after particular battles. Xiao He’s work cannot be described as a single dramatic encounter, since the essential feature was the regularity of repeated administrative tasks. An expedition’s field officers were visible in surviving accounts of battle, while the machinery that maintained food and reinforcements worked over much longer intervals. A shortage might originate far from a battlefield and still determine whether operations could continue. Because Xiao He had responsibility in Guanzhong, he was connected to that recurring problem of supply. His work occurred within a functioning community from which labor and food were gathered. Recognizing his role does not turn those social resources into an unlimited stock; it clarifies why continuing administration was part of the military story.

English editorial reading focus: Reducing burdens while keeping dependable principles (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

Early Western Han rulers governed a population that depended heavily on agricultural production while the state also needed resources to support administration. A land tax reduced the part of a harvest that a household could keep. Any decision to remit that revenue therefore affected both the farmers and the treasury, and the government had to consider how other obligations would continue. The Records of the Grand Historian reports that in the thirteenth year of Emperor Wen’s reign he ordered the removal of the land tax. The change addressed a specific fiscal burden rather than abolishing every tax or form of labor service. For the policy to affect actual households, local administrators had to apply the order to the relevant assessments. A decree at court and the amount collected in a rural district were connected but not identical steps. The record establishes the order and its stated policy context, not a complete account of gains received by every household. Other fiscal obligations remained. The episode consequently runs from concern over agriculture and the demands made upon cultivators, through an imperial tax decision, to its implementation as one part of a broader system of government finance. The historical sequence depends on several different kinds of action: an initial political or military problem, a response by people in positions to act, and an aftermath in which the arrangements still had to be implemented. 244爻 Case ID: XCASE-H41-L4 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-41-05 | Event ID: E39 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 損其疾，亦可喜也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「減除自己的毛病，迅速行動便有喜，無咎。」《象傳》解釋：同樣值得欣喜。

English editorial reading focus: Correcting one's own errors before trying to improve wider conditions (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

After the Shu campaign entered Longyou, the position at Jieting became critical to the continuation of Zhuge Liang’s first northern expedition. Ma Su was entrusted with local command. His deployment failed to hold the position, and the campaign could no longer proceed on its original assumptions. The importance of Jieting lay in its connection to the rest of the expedition, not simply in its name on a map. With Jieting lost, Zhuge Liang withdrew his forces. A withdrawal required soldiers and their officers to abandon the planned advance and return to a more defensible arrangement; the decision did not erase the costs already incurred. Zhuge Liang then submitted a memorial requesting a reduction of his own rank. The memorial acknowledged his responsibility for the choice of commander rather than assigning the entire failure to a subordinate. The military loss, the withdrawal, and the memorial were separate stages of the same episode. The surviving record supports this sequence, but it does not justify importing the fictional Empty Fort Stratagem into it. The episode also cannot establish that one appointment alone explained every aspect of the campaign’s failure. The site mattered because an advancing army could not move independently of its supporting positions. Once the approach became untenable, the remaining forces needed a withdrawal instead of continuing along the original route. The memorial is relevant precisely because it appears after the failure, when the commander was reviewing responsibility for decisions already made. Neither the act of retreating nor the statement of responsibility reverses the loss of the position. The command structure also mattered after the immediate battlefield reversal. The responsibility for appointing Ma Su was not identical to the responsibility for every action taken at Jieting, yet it was a decision Zhuge Liang could acknowledge in a formal document. When troops were withdrawn, that act changed the options available for the remaining expedition. The army could no longer pursue the same regional goals by the original sequence. This is why a full account connects the military reversal to the subsequent official response rather than treating the loss and the memorial as unrelated anecdotes.

245爻 Case ID: XCASE-H41-L5 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-41-06 | Event ID: E56 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 六五元吉，自上佑也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「有人增益他，價值十朋的大龜也不能違背，大吉。」《象傳》解釋：自上佑。

English editorial reading focus: Recognizing when outside help changes the possibilities (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

A succession conflict in the state of Jin forced Chong'er to leave the political position he had once occupied. With companions who remained alongside him, he spent years moving among other states. As an exile, he did not command the administrative and military resources of Jin. His situation depended on whether other rulers received him, offered provisions or chose to become involved in Jin's affairs. The treatment he received was not uniform. Some hosts offered assistance, while other encounters brought less favorable treatment. Throughout these travels, Chong'er and his followers had to maintain their association without a secure timetable for returning home. The record presents a succession of contacts and shifting circumstances, rather than a single, uninterrupted plan that carried him straight to the throne. There is no sound basis for assigning private thoughts to every host or for creating conversations missing from the surviving accounts. Eventually the state of Qin provided support that helped Chong'er return to Jin. He became ruler, later known as Duke Wen of Jin. His accession followed both the long period abroad and changes within Jin that made a return possible. Assistance from Qin mattered, but external backing alone would not explain every development within the state he was returning to. The order is important. First came the succession struggle and departure; then many years of movement, dependency and changing receptions; finally a political opening and Qin's assistance enabled a return and accession. His subsequent rule belongs to the aftermath, not to a destiny established on the day of his exile. Looking back from the eventual result can obscure how uncertain his position was during those years. The history supports a story of political displacement, enduring relationships and a later restoration, not a guarantee that every exile who waits will gain power. The aftermath must be distinguished from the original decision and evaluated from the surviving record.

246爻 Case ID: XCASE-H41-L6 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-41-07 | Event ID: E48 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 弗損益之，大得志也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「宜守正，出征則凶；不要損己，應增益他人。」《象傳》解釋：大得志。

English editorial reading focus: Building resources that serve a wider community (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

In the Warring States period, the Chengdu Plain faced the practical problems of supplying fields with water while managing the changing flow and sediment of the rivers. The irrigation works associated with Dujiangyan developed in this setting. Traditional accounts connect major work in the region with the Qin administration of Shu. Their significance lies in how water could be diverted and distributed, not merely in the construction of a single monumental structure. The system made use of the local terrain and moving water. Dividing the river's flow and handling sediment were connected operations: a scheme that delivered water to farms also had to prevent material from making channels unusable. Construction established a working arrangement, but it did not eliminate seasonal differences. Residents and officials needed to manage the system as weather, river levels and agricultural demands changed. The available summary does not supply a daily work diary or allow detailed speech to be attributed to individual engineers. Over time, the irrigation network supported cultivation and settlement in the plain. Its continued usefulness depended on maintenance, removal of sediment and the adjustment of channels and distribution. The responsibilities were spread across generations, rather than completed by one group at one moment. Not all fields or settlements necessarily had identical access to water, and a brief account cannot substitute for technical studies of every part of the network. The narrative therefore begins with the need to manage an important river, proceeds through the establishment of works that guided and allocated its waters, and extends into repeated repair and management after initial construction. The long history of Dujiangyan is one of continued operation as well as initial engineering. The classical image of the well is a later analogy applied in this collection; it is not evidence that the designers consulted this passage or used it as a set of engineering instructions.
